title: New Paxton recording exposes lingering GOP divisions in a tight Texas Senate race
description:
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton speaks during a campaign event in Houston, on September 21. - Antranik Tavitian/Getty Images
Ken Paxton has publicly said he would “love to have” John Cornyn’s support after their bruising Republican primary runoff in the Texas Senate race. But privately, Paxton has grown frustrated with the outgoing senator’s distance from his campaign.
“He’s clearly not helping. He wants me to lose,” the Texas attorney general said at a fundraiser last month, according to an audio recording obtained by CNN from an attendee who opposes Paxton.
fullText:
Ken Paxton has publicly said he would “love to have” John Cornyn’s support after their bruising Republican primary runoff in the Texas Senate race. But privately, Paxton has grown frustrated with the outgoing senator’s distance from his campaign.

“He’s clearly not helping. He wants me to lose,” the Texas attorney general said at a fundraiser last month, according to an audio recording obtained by CNN from an attendee who opposes Paxton.

While Paxton has minimized his criticism of Cornyn following their runoff, the private remarks demonstrate how their long-running tensions continue to roil the race, coming as national Republicans mount an all-out effort to help Paxton defeat Democratic state Rep. James Talarico. With polls showing a tight race, Republicans have poured well over $100 million into the general election in Texas, a state that has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994 but is now critical to Republican hopes of holding a Senate majority.

‘He wants me to lose’: Paxton complains about lack of support from Cornyn in leaked audio

Paxton made the comments at a September 24 gathering in Washington after receiving a question about Rep. Jasmine Crockett, the Democratic congresswoman whom Talarico defeated in his primary, according to two sources familiar with the discussion. The recording obtained by CNN begins with Paxton apparently referencing Crockett, who has not campaigned for Talarico, saying he does not “know how much she really affects votes.”

“I mean maybe a little bit around the margins, just like Cornyn, basically how much he affects me,” Paxton said.

After saying Cornyn wants him to lose, Paxton pointed to a recent encounter that he said a friend had with the senator at a Dallas restaurant. Paxton said the friend bought Cornyn’s table dessert and sought to thank him for “supporting the ticket” — and for “supporting Ken Paxton” — and Cornyn reacted angrily.

“Cornyn’s face went red. He backed off,” Paxton said. “He said, ‘Paxton’s gonna lose. We need to teach those Republicans a lesson. It’s going to be hard to learn, but they need to know that their decisions have consequences.’”

“That’s what he’s trying to do,” Paxton said. “That’s John Cornyn.”

CNN has not independently confirmed Paxton’s account, and a Cornyn representative, Rob Jesmer, told CNN that the conversation at the restaurant did not happen.

“If Sen. Cornyn wanted Ken to lose, I can assure you he’d be more active in the campaign,” Jesmer, a longtime political strategist for Cornyn, said. “He has said he supports the Republican ticket. Given all Ken has said and done, I think that’s a pretty good place for Sen. Cornyn to be.”

Asked for comment on the audio, Paxton’s campaign dismissed it as “a story that doesn’t exist” but noted that Paxton “has called, texted, and offered to have a conversation with Senator Cornyn.”

“Like all Texans, General Paxton appreciates his decades of service to the Lone Star State,” Paxton senior adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement. “We hope he will join us in our fight to preserve the institution that is the United States Senate and help save our majority.”

The two lobbyists who hosted the fundraising event, Chris Brinson and Susan Hirschmann, did not respond to requests for comment, nor did Talarico’s campaign.

A spokesperson for Crockett said she has taken a different approach than Cornyn since losing her own primary.

“Cornyn is the sitting senator and continues to attack his party’s nominee,” the spokesperson, Karrol Rimal, said in a statement. “Crockett endorsed Talarico on March 4th and has not stopped working to support Democrats across the nation since.”

Paxton’s problems with his own base, including former Cornyn supporters, have loomed over the final weeks of the race.

A Paxton campaign memo dated Tuesday, reported by Punchbowl News, told supporters that the “biggest challenge we face is shoring up Republicans following a bruising primary.”

A Fox News poll done late last month found that nearly a third of Republican likely voters had an unfavorable opinion of Paxton. While he was winning 90% of GOP voters, about a fifth of “non-MAGA” Republicans were breaking for Talarico.

The clip obtained by CNN is at least the fifth recording that has leaked from the fundraising event last month and put Paxton’s campaign on the defensive in the final weeks of the race. Previous clips have featured Paxton saying the GOP’s midterm convention damaged him politically and that he feels like he has lost “control” over his campaign as outside groups have handled most of the spending.

title: 4 players to watch for Oklahoma this week against Texas
description: 4 players to watch for OU-Texas.
fullText:
The Oklahoma Sooners and the Texas Longhorns will renew the annual Red River Rivalry clash on Saturday, and an underdog OU team is far from healthy coming into that game. The initial SEC availability report, released Wednesday night, listed 13 OU players, compared to 4 Texas players. Oklahoma had several players upgraded to probable on Thursday night, but still there's doubt about the availability of two starters for the offensive line.

With all of those injuries, several players will be asked to step up in a big-time environment. Texas is the No. 1 team in the nation, and they'll have no mercy for their arch-rival this weekend. Oklahoma is looking to shock the world, and it'll need some big performances to make that happen.

Here are four players to watch for Oklahoma against Texas.

OU has its two starting cornerbacks healthy for this game: Eli Bowen and Courtland Guillory. However, the third cornerback, Jacobe Johnson, is out with an injury. That means Trystan Haynes will likely a lot more action in Dallas.

Haynes has been part of the backup rotation at cornerback, but he hasn't been on the field a lot so far this season. With Texas' deep rotation of wide receivers, led by Cam Coleman and Ryan Wingo, the cornerbacks are going to have their work cut out for them this week. That includes Haynes, in what could be his most significant action as a Sooner.

Oklahoma's offensive line has been banged up this season, and that only got worse over the bye week. Starting left tackle Michael Fasusi (doubtful this week) hasn't played since 12 snaps against UTEP. Now, starting left guard Eddy Pierre-Louis is questionable for this week. Year after year, OU has key injuries up front that they have to work through.

If Fasusi can't go, Ryan Fodje will start at left tackle again. If Pierre-Louis can't play, it'll likely be Heath Ozaeta at left guard. Jake Maikkula is the center, Noah Best should stay at right guard, and E'Marion Harris is again in line to play right tackle.

Other reserves like Caleb Nitta, Peyton Joseph, and Deacon Schmitt could be called upon as well. Ozaeta is a veteran who can play either guard spot, and he is the only player who played a pivotal role during the 2024 debacle that is still left in 2026. Against a very good Texas front line, the offensive line will be under scrutiny this week.

OU's linebackers aren't fully healthy either. While Kip Lewis is off the injury report, Owen Heinecke and Cole Sullivan are probable. That means James Nesta could once again see a larger role.

Nesta has been asked to step up during a myriad of linebacker injuries this season, and he's played a few different spots as the only one of the top four players who has been able to stay fully healthy. He may see some time at Cheetah this week, although Reggie Powers III is still the starter at that position. Still, Nesta's continued growth and relative inexperience will be put to the test on Saturday.

Peyton Bowen, one of OU's starting safeties, has been excellent to begin this season, However, his running mate, Michael Boganowski, still hasn't played since the Michigan game. He was initially listed as questionable against UT but upgraded to probable on Thursday night, so it could be Omarion Robinson starting again in the secondary next to Bowen.

Robinson was expected to be a big part of the safety group this year, but has taken on an even larger role for the last two-and-a-half games. Against Texas, he'll be targeted some, as the least-experienced member of the starting OU defensive backfield. Even if Boganowski plays, Robinson will surely get a steady diet of snaps this week. The Longhorns have a very diverse offense that tricks your eyes, so Robinson has to play well as one of the last lines of defense.

title: Oklahoma vs Texas picks, predictions, odds for Week 6 college football
description: Here are our predictions for Oklahoma's matchup with Texas in the Red River Rivalry on Saturday.
fullText:
NORMAN — Oklahoma faces No. 1 Texas in the annual Red River Rivalry on Saturday at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas.

The Sooners and the Longhorns will meet for the 122nd time. Since 1929, the programs have played annually at Fair Park in Dallas and have played inside the Cotton Bowl every year since 1937.

OU has won five of its last eight meetings against Texas, 11 of the last 17 and 17 of the last 27. But the Sooners are 8.5-point underdogs and coach Brent Venables is at risk of falling to 1-4 against OU's archrival.

The last time the Sooners defeated an AP No. 1 team was in 2007 when OU defeated Missouri, 38-17.

Still, some believe the Sooners can pull off an historic upset. Here are our predictions for this year's game:

More: For OU football coach Brent Venables, pressure 'comes with the territory' against Texas

Sooner defense takes the fight to the Longhorns, but the burnt orange outlasts the crimson and cream late. OU wins the turnover battle (shocking!) but fails to run well enough against the Texas defense.

This is nothing more than a gut feel. Texas is the better team, but we've seen Brent Venables' Sooners come through in must-win games. Remember last November? OU will have a chance so long as John Mateer holds onto the football.

Let's play the old iffin' game at the Cotton Bowl. If John Mateer can match his stats from the Georgia game but not have any turnovers ... if the OU offensive line can overcome Michael Fasusi's absence ... if Isaiah Sategna can break a punt return for a touchdown ... then this OU defense can remind everyone it's elite enough to pull out the win.

OU's defense should match up well against a Texas offense that hasn't been spectacular. The Longhorns rank 102nd nationally in EPA per rush while the Sooners' defense is fifth best in the country in EPA allowed per rush. UT has also committed 19 penalties in its last two games. If OU doesn't turn the ball over, it has a fair shake to shock the country.

Don't expect a lot of points with both elite defenses in this game. That gives the edge to Arch Manning and Co. to again steal a game late with a long drive.

title: The flu sidelines James Talarico at a crucial moment in the Texas Senate race
description:
Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has been off the campaign trail, sick with the flu. (Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call via Getty)
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.
But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days. 
His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend.
fullText:
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.

But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days.

His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend.

While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.

It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date.

“We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.”

While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation.

“He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event.

“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”

Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail.

“After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.”

Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him.

Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem.

“Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.”

Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election.

Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence.

“It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.”

To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention.

At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail.

“You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said Wednesday at a rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”

After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton.

“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social.

It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though he’s not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media:

“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX.”

fullText:
SAN ANTONIO (AP) — President Donald Trump, facing protesters and a poor political climate, fought to rally Texas voters behind Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Wednesday night in a bid to stave off sweeping Democratic victories in the nation's most populous red state.

But Trump's remarks were not focused solely on Paxton.

Speaking to a packed Freeman Coliseum, Trump also pledged to award retired baseball star Roger Clemens the Presidential Medal of Freedom, restated his support for the death penalty for drug dealers and clarified recent comments in which he talked about the possibility of Iran bombing American cities as part of a recurring riff about how high fuel costs are "a small price to pay" for the war.

"You want to see problems? Let them hit San Diego, let them hit Los Angeles," Trump said. "We're not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country."

The president's message was interrupted repeatedly by protesters, including by one who appeared to be close to the stage. In all, at least a dozen demonstrators interrupted the president. Some were led away by police.

Trump stepped away from the microphone briefly after one interruption.

"He's going back home to mom," Trump said. "But what he doesn't know is his mom voted for Trump."

The Republican Party did not plan to devote so much money and manpower to Texas this midterm season.

Texas is the nation's most populous reliably Republican state, where Trump won in 2024 by almost 14 percentage points. But with Election Day less than a month away, Trump's poor approval ratings, the Iran war and soaring gas prices have threatened Republicans in virtually every state.

Wednesday's appearance marked Trump's third trip to Texas in less than a month, and party officials have devoted more than $300 million to elections in the state so far.

In a sign of Trump's poor standing, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott did not attend the evening rally. A three-term Republican governor who won reelection in 2022 by roughly 11 percentage points, even Abbott has been caught in the turbulent national currents.

He's locked in a competitive reelection race against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

Instead of appearing with Trump, Abbott was scheduled to attend the dedication of a hospital about 330 miles away. Democrats seized on the governor's absence.

"For years, Greg Abbott has never been shy about embracing Donald Trump, calling Trump a 'great friend' and championing his agenda every step of the way," said Texas Democratic Party spokesperson Jacob Long. "But now, as Texas families get crushed by record-high prices driven by Trump's tariffs and war with Iran, suddenly Greg Abbott has somewhere else to be."

While the race for governor has drawn a sudden influx of cash from Democrats, the state's U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention as Democrats fight for the chamber's majority. The state has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, but candidate James Talarico's fundraising, Trump's low approval rating and nagging concerns about Paxton's character have put the race squarely in play.

Trump spent most of his remarks focused on the Senate contest, describing Paxton as "perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America."

"He was tough and he was with us all the way," Trump said of Paxton, whom he endorsed in the state's GOP primary over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn. "He's a fantastic man."

Trump made no mention of the recently leaked recording of Paxton lamenting the war in Iran and rising fuel prices, while also complaining his campaign was being run by operatives in Washington.

He repeatedly criticized Talarico, including on the death penalty, a point that would appeal to many conservatives in the state that leads the nation in executions.

Trump restated his support for the death penalty for "large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer," while acknowledging that Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad.

The president approved the method of execution earlier this week and suggested that Talarico opposes it.

The Talarico campaign did not immediately respond when asked about the candidate's position on Hasan's scheduled execution.

Paxton, invited onstage near the end of the rally, heaped praise on Trump, who stood behind him: "I am so grateful that you're here."

While Trump promoted Paxton briefly at the beginning of his remarks, he spent almost as much time later talking up Clemens, the retired Red Sox and Yankees pitcher who has been denied a spot in Major League Baseball's Hall of Fame due to his alleged involvement with performance-enhancing drugs.

Trump brought him onstage and said he'd be awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, which is the highest civilian honor — and, Trump said, "a step up" from the Hall of Fame.

Clemens said he was stunned by the honor.

"This supersedes anything that obviously I've done in my playing career," he said, standing alongside Trump. "And to get it from this man, this president. ... You talking about a winner? That's a winner right there."

Peoples reported from New York and Beaumont reported from Des Moines, Iowa. Associated Press writer Will Weissert in Washington contributed.

fullText:
The United States military has had 81 aircraft destroyed or damaged in the war with Iran, a Congressional Research Service report released this week says.

The number includes both airplanes and helicopters as well as drones, with the MQ-9 Reaper drone – used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, close air support and combat search and rescue – accounting for more than half of the losses.

But also on the list are some of the Pentagon’s most-prized assets, including an F-35A fighter jet and an E-3 Sentry, the four-engine jet with a large radar dome atop the fuselage used for target tracking and airspace management.

The total cost of the aircraft lost is between $1.9 billion and $3.3 billion, depending on the Defense Department’s plans for replacements, the report said, citing figures from the Congressional Budget Office.

The total cost of the war is much higher – at least $45 billion, sources have told CNN. That figure doesn’t include damage to infrastructure at US bases in the region, including those where some of the aircraft losses happened.

Some of the aircraft included in the count may have been returned to service, including eight F-15 Strike Eagle fighter jets that sustained light damage in an Iranian strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, Jordan, in September.

The report is based on numbers contained in statements from the Defense Department; its inspector general; US Central Command, which has been conducting the operations against Iran; and news reports reviewed by the CRS.

The report poses several questions for congressional consideration, including whether lawmakers are getting enough information from the Pentagon on the losses to determine effects and remedies.

Defense Department reporting on Iran war losses has, to date, been vague. Even the Pentagon inspector general’s report on the losses, released in September, and covering action from February 28 to June 30, cites previous CRS reports for some of its aircraft loss numbers.

Other issues Congress needs to think about are whether to provide funding for repairs or replacements; whether there is enough industrial capacity to satisfy those requirements; and the effects on US military sales to foreign partners.

It also raises questions about how the Iran war has affected US posture outside the Middle East.

“Congress may assess whether losses in certain high-demand platforms that are aging and limited in number, such as the E-3 Sentry, create capability gaps or increase risk in other theaters,” the report says.

Analysts have said actions in the Middle East, including the Iran war and earlier confrontations with the Houthi rebels in Yemen, an Iranian proxy group, have taken an especially heavy toll on the MQ-9 drones, which Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told Congress earlier this year was the military’s “most valuable player” in the war with Iran.

Forty-five have been lost in the Middle East this year, “an alarming rate,” according to a September report from the Atlantic Council.

The Air Force has lost about 35% of its MQ-9s since 2004, it says.

title: Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh's struggling unit gets called out
description: For years, Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh’s exceptional track record allowed him to largely escape blame, even when the Sooners struggled to score. He's getting plenty of criticism heading into Saturday's game against Texas in Dallas
fullText:
Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh's struggling unit gets called out originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

NORMAN, Okla. -- For years, Oklahoma offensive line coach Bill Bedenbaugh's exceptional track record allowed him to largely escape blame, even when the Sooners struggled to score.

He earned that pass with a lengthy run of success. He has coached 14 NFL draft picks since joining the staff in 2013, including NFL stars Orlando Brown and Creed Humphrey. He was a finalist for the Broyles Award as the nation's top assistant coach in 2017 and a semifinalist in 2018. His lines have blocked for Heisman-winning quarterbacks Baker Mayfield and Kyler Murray.

Times have changed. Bedenbaugh is getting plenty of heat heading into Saturday's game against Texas in Dallas amidst a stretch of three games during which the Sooners have scored a combined 37 points, failed to break 300 yards and lost twice.

Even the media is acting differently. Generally, when there have been questions about the offense, reporters have focused on skill players. Now, Bedenbaugh's offensive line is a primary target, along with offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle.

Venables didn't protect Bedenbaugh or the unit when asked about the offensive line on Tuesday.

"It's been incredibly inconsistent, very disappointing," Venables said.

Here's Brent Venables today being brutally honest about the state of Oklahoma's offensive line: "It's been incredibly inconsistent and very disappointing. As you build your football team, that's a critical place. That is a place that probably requires the most development of any position that you have on your roster." "Very uneven job when it comes to choosing the guys that we've brought in here. Way too many guys are coming and going at that position group...It's been very unstable and certainly not the kind of development that you want from top to bottom." #Sooners:

Venables said one factor in the offensive line's struggles is that players switch schools so often that it is hard to develop players, which negates one of Bedenbaugh's greatest strengths. He also said because so many players bounce around, building continuity is difficult.

"That is a place that probably requires the most development at any position that you have on your roster and we haven't allowed, for lots of different reasons … the portal's the No. 1 reason," Venables said.

Venables said it's not all on Bedenbaugh. He hinted that some of the offensive linemen missing games are "injured players" who should be on the field.

"Some guys -- that guy's always hurt," Venables said. "And so if you look at, just peel it back on our roster, you can figure out who maybe that's been."

Peeling it back, left tackle Michael Fasusi has missed three games and most of the other with a shoulder injury, center Jake Maikkula has missed one game (knee) and right guard Ryan Fodje (knee) has missed one game. Fasusi was listed as doubtful for the Texas game on Wednesday's SEC injury report and left guard Eddy Pierre-Louis is listed as questionable with an undisclosed injury.

title: Texas executes man using same drug involved in Christa Pike's failed lethal injection
description:
— A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee’s failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.
Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m.
fullText:
HUNTSVILLE, Texas (AP) — A Texas man who fatally shot a convenience store clerk was put to death Wednesday evening, becoming the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year and the first since Tennessee's failed attempt to administer a lethal injection to Christa Pike a week ago.

Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. after receiving a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville. He was convicted of killing Vickie Swartout, 42, in a 2000 store robbery caught on surveillance video.

Asked by the warden if he had a final statement, Howard apologized profusely to some members of his victim's family, who watched through a window just feet from the death chamber.

"I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness," he said, shortly before the injection got underway. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

He also thanked his friends and family and said he loved them, adding he was "in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y'all." He concluded with: "Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y'all."

As the pentobarbital began taking effect, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped. He then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, each time the sound becoming quieter. Within about 30 seconds, all movement stopped.

He was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.

His sister was among witnesses watching through a window from an adjacent room and became distraught, exclaiming several times: "Get me out of here." She was assisted by corrections officers in exiting the witness room.

Texas has executed seven people so far in 2026, including Howard, and plans two more executions later this year.

Howard's attorneys unsuccessfully sought to block the execution by arguing that he was intellectually disabled and that he faced risks similar to those in Pike's case because both states use pentobarbital for lethal injections.

Pike's lawyers continue to seek more information about what went wrong after the 50-year-old woman survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30. Her lawyers said she was unconscious at a hospital after the attempt but was awake and speaking by Tuesday.

Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during the robbery. Evidence presented at trial included surveillance video showing Howard shooting Swartout.

Howard, who was 20 at the time, took $114 and a carton of cigarettes from the store in Silsbee, a small, rural town about 100 miles (160 kilometers) northeast of Houston, according to court records.

In bidding to halt Howard's execution, his attorneys had filed a motion hours earlier before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals raising concerns about the quality of Texas' execution drugs. The court denied that request and a second filing involving the drugs without comment.

His attorneys also argued unsuccessfully to the U.S. Supreme Court that Howard's execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. The Supreme Court in 2002 had barred the execution of intellectually disabled people, though it gave states some discretion in determining such disabilities.

The state told the court that Howard's lawyers did not present evidence that would show he meets the requirements for a claim of intellectual disability.

The high court late Wednesday declined to intervene, without comment, clearing the way for the execution.

Florida has carried out 16 executions so far this year, the most of any state. Most states that allow executions use lethal injection as their primary method.

Tennessee Republican Gov. Bill Lee has halted the one remaining execution that was scheduled to be carried out in his state this year.

Stengle reported from Fort Worth, Texas.

title: Army sets date for Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan to face firing squad

fullText:
It will be the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years.

Nidal Hasan, who was sentenced to death for the 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3, according to a memo from the acting Army secretary.

The execution, the first carried out by the U.S. military in more than 60 years, is scheduled for 1 p.m. CT, according to the memo issued Tuesday by acting Army Secretary Adam Telle.

The Pentagon announced Monday that Hasan would be executed by firing squad after President Donald Trump approved the decision Friday.

Under the military’s execution process for prisoners on death row, the Army secretary initiates the proceedings, which then require approval from the defense secretary and eventually the president.

Under Army policy, executions must happen within 150 days of the president approving it, but no sooner than 60 days.

The military has not executed a service member since 1961, when Pvt. John Bennett was put to death after being convicted of the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl in Austria.

On Nov. 5, 2009, Hasan, then an Army psychiatrist, opened fire at the Soldier Readiness Processing Center at the Fort Hood military base, killing 12 soldiers and one civilian before he was shot, severely wounded and arrested.

Hasan was convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder and sentenced to death in 2013. He was sent to a military detention center at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.

He is one of four death row inmates in the Army justice system.

The announcement of his execution comes after ABC News reported in June that the Army had been planning military executions, according to internal documents and officials familiar with the matter.

Army regulation dictates that at least two media outlets should be selected to witness the execution.

title: Former Army major who killed 13 in Fort Hood shooting to be executed by firing squad

"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on X.
fullText:
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army major who killed 13 people in a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, will be executed by firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday.

"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell wrote on X.

He added, "The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come."

The U.S. military has not carried out an execution since 1961 and has not used a firing squad to execute a service member since World War II.

The announcement of Trump's approval came days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection. The failed execution prompted Tennessee's governor to halt further executions this year and order a third-party review.

Asked whether the failed execution in Tennessee would lead him to seek changes to capital punishment, Trump called it "an interesting situation." He told reporters in Denton, Texas, that carrying out lethal injections "shouldn't be very difficult."

Trump's approval sets in motion a series of procedural steps toward carrying out Hasan's execution. But Hasan could put the process on hold — potentially for years — by filing a habeas corpus appeal challenging the legality of his detention in the civilian federal court system, according to an article published in May in the magazine Army Lawyer.

Hasan was convicted in a 2013 court-martial of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and was sentenced to death. He exhausted his regular appeals in 2025.

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, walked into the Soldier Readiness Processing Center, where soldiers were undergoing medical checkups before deploying, and witnesses testified he shouted "Allahu akbar" — Arabic for "God is great!" — before he opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun. He killed 13 people and wounded more than 30.

According to the Associated Press, Hasan said he carried out the shooting to stop soldiers from going to Afghanistan and killing his fellow Muslims.

He represented himself at his 2013 court-martial and mounted little defense, telling jurors that evidence would show he was the shooter and describing himself as a soldier who had "switched sides."

The Pentagon did not explain why Hasan would be executed by firing squad rather than lethal injection, the method specified in the military's current execution regulations. It also did not say whether those regulations would need to change.

The Army adopted a plan in February for carrying out military executions at the federal government's execution facility in Terre Haute, Ind., ABC News reported in June.

Known as Operation Resolute Justice, the plan calls for condemned service members to be transferred there from the military prison at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., and for the Army to coordinate with the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The Army is to be ready to carry out an execution no sooner than 60 days and within 150 days of presidential approval. ABC's report did not specify an execution method.

The Justice Department separately directed the Bureau of Prisons in April to expand its protocol for federal civilian executions to include methods beyond lethal injection, including firing squads. That change does not apply to military executions.

Firing squads have also recently returned at the state level. Five states allow them, according to the Death Penalty Information Center: Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina and Utah.

Idaho made the firing squad its primary execution method on July 1 after a law signed in 2025 took effect. South Carolina carried out three firing squad executions in 2025, the first uses of the method in the U.S. since 2010. Condemned prisoners there can choose among authorized execution methods.

After Pike's failed execution, several top Republicans in Tennessee said they want to explore alternative ways of executing condemned prisoners.

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, told the AP, "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully."

Top legislative leaders have already spoken with Blackburn about potential changes to state execution laws during their 2027 session.

"We want to broaden it, include more methods," Tennessee House Speaker Cameron Sexton said. "What those are as of today, I'm not sure. But I don't think there's any method that's off the table at this point."

Death sentences are extremely rare in the military justice system, and executions are even rarer. Four men, including Hasan, are currently on the military's death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kan.

President George W. Bush approved the execution of Army Spc. Ronald Gray in 2008, but a judge put it on hold. Gray remains at Fort Leavenworth.

The last person executed under the military justice system was Pvt. John Bennett, who was hanged in 1961 for the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.

title: OU football QB John Mateer used Sooners' bye week to 'reset' and silence doubters
description: Following a bye week that served as a much-needed rest, OU football quarterback John Mateer is looking to prove everyone wrong come Saturday against Texas.
fullText:
NORMAN — The bye week was a breath of fresh air for John Mateer.

Oklahoma's quarterback has endured constant criticism after a disappointing start to the season and used the time off last week to recenter, assess what has gone wrong through four weeks and spend time with his teammates, who have reinforced their belief in their leader.

"I had a good break personally," Mateer said after practice Monday. "We had great practices, hung out with some of the guys. Went out to dinner. It was a reset because (during the season), you don't really get time to — you do, but not as much as the offseason."

Mateer knows what's at stake this week.

OU football bowl projections 2026: Where are Sooners entering Texas game?

A year after he put his all into returning for this game — the Red River Rivalry against Texas — 17 days post-surgery, Mateer finds himself up against it again. His confidence was clearly shot after turning the ball over on three consecutive drives in a blowout road loss to Georgia in which his coaches pondered benching him.

He knows he must improve and take care of the ball to give the Sooners any shot against the No. 1-ranked Longhorns on Saturday at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas. Mateer's turnovers have been catastrophic for OU after his interception against Michigan all but sealed a Wolverines win and his two fumbles against Georgia resulted in two Bulldogs touchdowns.

Last season's Texas game when he threw three interceptions is one he still thinks about. Not so much because of what it took to play but about how he played and how he wears that loss.

"We're ready to go," Mateer said. "Everybody, you get to sit back and look at where we're at, and we're ready to go. I'm more excited. It's the game, it is what everybody says it is. It's awesome and I'm honored to play in it, in a rivalry and for this team and for these guys.

"Last year, it was what it was. It's taught me a lot but I'm standing here and ready to play this week."

Here’s #Sooners QB John Mateer on the bye week, Red River Rivalry and where his confidence is at. pic.twitter.com/HVgZIOu7o2

Mateer has stayed off social media so he hasn't heard the constant negativity surrounding his play. But he undeniably feels it.

He has a good support system around him that has helped him through this over the last several weeks. OU certainly has devoted all of its resources to help every player but especially Mateer as he endures this rut.

There have been thoughts that his play might fracture the team or divide one unit against another. That hasn't been the case at all as the Sooners' leaders have rallied around Mateer.

"The fact that I haven't performed is disappointing, but I'm blessed to play ball today and to get better," Mateer said. "It's a kids game that we all take really seriously, and I'm honored to stand here and be this person in this position. But you come out to practice today knowing that it's everything I've ever dreamed of.

"So even when you struggle and you get judged, it's because I've done good in the past to put me (where) something is expected from me — from me and from other people. It's the position I'm in, but I'm learning."

More: Will disgruntled OU football fans air their grievances during Red River Rivalry?

Mateer said this offseason how much it meant to him when general manager Jim Nagy and coach Brent Venables reaffirmed their commitment to him after an up-and-down 2025 season. Venables did it once again last week, announcing Mateer is still OU's starter.

Whether or not anyone else does, it's clear the Sooners still believe Mateer gives them the best chance to win. That could change Saturday.

Following the bye week, Mateer is ready to attack this week of practice and focus on improving as much as he can before Saturday. For someone who needs all the help he can get with getting his confidence back to where it needs to be, the support he's gotten around him means the world.

He has a chance to silence all of the doubters Saturday.

"It helps, it really does," Mateer said. "The tight ends came over Sunday after the game and watched some football. I appreciate that. And the receivers, we're talking ball and just hanging out and they say it. (Defensive ends coach Miguel Chavis), he's been great, and (offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle), (quarterbacks coach John Kuceyeski) and Coach Venables.

" ... He tells me straight up, like, he has my back and he's proud of the work and the toughness, and I appreciate that more than he knows, more than I can say."

At the time, Hasan requested a delay in court proceedings so he could ready a new legal strategy that would show he acted "in defense of others."

Asked by presiding Judge Col. Tara Osborn who he was defending, Hasan replied, "The leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban."

Hasan was convicted by a military jury in August 2013, which recommended he be sentenced to death.

title: The Texas-Oklahoma rivalry can change things quickly, regardless of teams' records
description: A year after Texas entered the game with two losses, the roles have flipped. Kirk Bohls explains why the Red River rivalry can turn quickly.
fullText:
AUSTIN - The storylines are pretty much the same this October.

That's how fast things can change in one of the most historic rivalries in the sport.

Texas has raised itself from the ashes after reaching the heights of the Mack Brown era. Oklahoma was running things in the Big 12 and grabbing Heisman trophies like they were pocket change before running afoul of late.

Texas reached the College Football Playoff semifinals two straight seasons from 2023-24 before sitting out the playoffs last year. OU hadn't been a contender recently but did crash the CFP party last December only to exit quickly despite leading Alabama 17-0 in Norman in the first round.

We turn to the present season. Texas is up, OU is down. But check back in a week where fortunes can change at breakneck speed.

Texas, most would probably agree, isn't the best team in college football, but it is unbeaten and ranked No. 1 because of quality wins. That's why it is a 7½-point favorite.

Oklahoma, everyone would attest, isn't close to the best team, either, or maybe not even one of the really good teams in college football, but there are few programs as proud or as successful as the Sooners, and they might actually be good with two quality losses.

And to be honest, none of that really matters when it comes to October in Dallas where Stonie Clark can become a hero with one monumental tackle at the goal-line and Peter Gardere stamps his legacy as a quarterback with four wins over OU. Players can enter the Cotton Bowl as a mortal and leave 60 minutes later as a legend.

BOHLS: Nine things and one crazy prediction

Who knows what qualifies as an upset any more in a series that has been played in Dallas since 1912 and at the State Fair since 1929 and is more passion play than sport. The Longhorns lead the series 65-51-5, but there are good reasons Texas ranks fifth in all-time football wins at 975 and OU sixth with 967.

"I can promise you one thing," Texas coach Steve Sarkisian said, "nobody's overlooking anybody in this game."

That's the perfect history lesson since these two teams have flipped the scripts from just 12 months ago.

A year ago the wounded Longhorns limped into the Cotton Bowl unranked with two losses.

On Saturday, the flawed Sooners will sneak into that historic area unranked with two losses.

Before this game in 2025, Texas had lost to one of the college football foremost bluebloods on the road (Ohio State) and was embarrassed in its SEC opener (at Florida).

This year, OU has lost to one of the heavyweight brands in the nation on the road (Michigan) and was humiliated in its SEC opener (at Georgia).

While the two teams appear to be trending in opposite directions, their emotions will identically coincide this weekend. Nothing changes that.

Both squads will be at a fever pitch for Saturday's 2:45 p.m. kickoff. Actually even before that.

"There's always a ton of emotion in pregame for whatever reason," Sarkisian acknowledged. "The ball's not kicked off, and everybody's all hyped up at the start of the game."

Sarkisian said he and his staff will try to temper those emotions, nerves and unbridled anticipation and stay focused on the game itself.

Texas didn't do that all that well last October when it trailed 6-3 at intermission, but rallied to shut out the Sooners 20-0 in the second half to seal its second consecutive win in this series and third in four years.

That's usually how this series flows. One side dominates for a span, only to be ultimately switched. Just ask Mack Brown.

Sarkisian doesn't really He attributes the Sooners' 2-2 record largely to being a product of a harsh schedule, but of course the last thing he wants to do is rile up the crimson fan base.

"I don't know that necessarily they haven't played well," said Sarkisian, who is personally 3-2 against the Sooners. "Defensively, they've played exceptional. These guys are a phenomenal defensive football team. They played at Michigan, which is not easy. They played at Georgia, which we know is not easy. I'm sure Coach (Brent) Venables wishes he had the schedule of some other teams or they could be 4-0."

While the Longhorns appear to have much more to play for with a terrific start at a championship run with two quality wins over Ohio State and Tennessee, the Sooners will approach this game with an anger level and desperation that could mask any shortage of offensive firepower or momentum.

Mix in a slow start with a turnover here and there, and up may become down. Worked for Texas last year.

That's just how this rivalry rolls.

"They're definitely going to give us their best effort," Longhorn linebacker Justin Cryer said. "I think they are super dynamic (on offense). But I don't take a lot from their recent performances and people's perception of them. This is a game they're going to show up for. We have to be on it or it's going to be a long day for us."

That type of response has to be music to Sarkisian's ears.

He gave his players, which include 48 newcomers to his roster, a tutorial on Texas-OU 101 to educate them about the history and significance of the only rivalry in the country that splits the stadium down the middle with rival fans sitting side by side at the two 50-yard lines. You know, within spitting range.

Heck, he even showed them a picture of the storied Cotton Bowl and pointed out the tunnel from which both teams enter the playing field and where they will warm up.

"But at the end of the day," he said, "it's football, and the game means a ton to us. I don't waste a lot of time and energy in the rah-rah speeches on a Monday."

For his money, he loves the neutral-site setting of this game, which will be played for the 122nd time. Thankfully, he appreciates the history and doesn't ever want to go to a home-and-home arrangement.

"The idea that this thing's split at the 50, and half the game is a home game, and the other time it's a road game when you're in OU's end, I love all of that," Sarkisian said. "I love all that comes with it. I love that it's at the State Fair. The smell of the corn dogs, the funnel cakes and all that, it's so special and so unique, and I do not take that lightly. I would not change it for anything."

That's one thing that should never change, even if the programs' trajectories do.

There's more to Houston with the Chronicle.

title: Who is Michele Tafoya? Ex-sideline reporter aims to turn Minnesota red in Senate race.
description:

Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red.
fullText:
When it comes to the battle for control of the U.S. Senate, Republicans are mostly playing defense. The lion's share of the races that will decide which party secures a majority in November are in red states — including Texas, Iowa and Ohio — where the GOP is hoping to hold on against ascendant Democratic challengers.

Minnesota is one of the few states in the country where the party is in a position to go on offense and potentially turn a blue seat red.

In pursuit of that goal, the GOP has put its hopes in Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster and NFL sideline reporter turned politician who polls suggest has a real chance of winning in a state that has been dominated by Democrats in recent election cycles.

Tafoya is running for the seat currently held by Democrat Tina Smith, who is not pursuing re-election. Instead her opponent will be Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flannagan, a progressive who supports policies like Medicare for All and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Minnesota has been at the center of some of the biggest controversies of President Trump's second term, particularly his administration's sweeping immigration crackdown. Though a majority of Minnesotans disapprove of Trump's performance as president, Tafoya has steadily chipped away at Flanagan's lead in polls since the primary.

Here's what you need to know about who she is, what she stands for and how she went from the sidelines to the center of one of the midterms' most pivotal races.

Tafoya was born and raised in Southern California. Her father was an aeronautical engineer, and her mother was a school teacher. She has Hispanic heritage on her father's side.

She married her husband, Mark Vandersall, in 2000. They have two children. Tafoya has been open about her struggles with infertility, which included several miscarriages. Her daughter, Oliva, was adopted from Colombia as a nod to her father's lineage.

After launching her sports broadcasting career in Los Angeles, she moved to Minnesota in the early 1990s to take a job at the KFAN sports radio station in Minneapolis. Before long, she moved on to a national role with CBS, which proved to be the jumping-off point for a decades-long career that made her one of the country's most recognizable sports broadcasters. She covered five Super Bowls, the NBA and the Olympics — winning five Emmys for her work along the way.

Tafoya's last broadcast was during Super Bowl LVI in 2022. Her political career began the very next day. Less than 12 hours after the game ended, she announced that she would co-chair the campaign of Republican Kendall Qualls in his bid to become Minnesota governor.

Tafoya has said she always had strong political views, but made a specific effort to keep them out of her work as a broadcaster.

"I was not as free to be as vocal about world events that I'm concerned about," she told The Athletic in 2022. "It's not because I was told to shut up. I want to be very clear about that. But look, if you're on a show like Sunday Night Football … the last thing they want to do is invite controversy."

Tafoya was more open about her beliefs outside on social media, where she would regularly promote work from conservative outlets. But she also made statements that broke from the GOP mainstream, including support for efforts to curb climate change. In an interview with Sports Illustrated in 2015, she described herself as a "pro-choice" conservative with "definite libertarian strains."

After retiring from broadcasting, Tafoya made several appearances as a speaker at Republican political events, including the Conservative Political Action Conference. She was also a guest host on The View, taking on the role of the conservative-leaning voice in contrast to the show's more liberal regular panelists.

In 2022, Tafoya launched a podcast that frequently touched on political topics and featured Republican politicians as guests. The most recent episode, released in January, includes an interview with former My Pillow CEO Mike Lindell, who unsuccessfully ran for Minnesota governor this year despite an endorsement from President Trump.

Tafoya formally announced her Senate bid a few weeks later. In August, she comfortably won a crowded Republican primary to set up a head-to-head race against Flanagan in November.

In her pitch to Minnesota voters, Tafoya has leaned into her sports background.

"I'm not gonna stay on the sidelines any longer," she said while standing on a snow-covered football field in her campaign announcement video.

For years, I walked the sidelines when the stakes were the highest, and that job taught me how leadership really works.I'm running for U.S. Senate to bring that experience to Washington and deliver the real results Minnesota deserves. https://t.co/vDbHWpAXg9

— Michele Tafoya (@Michele_Tafoya) January 21, 2026

Like other swing-state Republicans across the country, Tafoya has worked to find a balance between supporting Trump and pushing back on some of his most unpopular policies.

She has supported the president throughout the war with Iran, at one point telling Minnesotans to "take one less trip to Starbucks" to help offset the rising cost of gas. More recently, though, she has joined a growing list of GOP candidates who have called for Trump to end the conflict.

"No president of either party should have a blank check to wage war without the consent of Congress or the buy-in of the American people. That includes President Donald Trump," Tafoya told Twin Cities local news KSTP on Saturday.

Tafoya added that she would be "inclined to vote to end this war" if given the opportunity in the Senate. She has also said she didn't agree with ICE's tactics in Minneapolis and described Trump's tariff policies as "hit or miss."

Her policy views mostly align with mainstream Republican positions. She backs strong immigration enforcement and Trump's mass deportation campaign, a "tough on crime" approach to public safety, tax cuts, and laws barring transgender athletes from competing in women's and girls' sports. On abortion, she says she agrees with the Supreme Court's decision overturning Roe v. Wade, but personally believes there should be "reasonable access" in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy.

Tafoya's own opinions of Trump have evolved as well. In 2022, she published an open letter urging Trump not to run for a second term, describing his previous time in the White House as "absolute mayhem." She also said on her podcast around the same time that there was much about Trump that she found "difficult to accept."

But during the 2024 presidential campaign, Tafoya said she was supporting Trump with "more enthusiasm" than before. She also said she felt "sort of agnostic" on the Jan. 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol. She celebrated Trump's victory later that year, describing it as "morning in America" — a reference to Ronald Reagan's famous phrase from the 1980s.

Tafoya has mostly left Trump out of her current campaign ads and speeches, instead focusing her messaging on issues like fraud, affordability and public safety. The president opted not to endorse a candidate in Minnesota's Republican primary and has yet to throw his support behind Tafoya in the general election.

Tafoya is one of the few Republicans in major races across the country who is outperforming expectations in the polls.

title: Inside the Numbers: Texas stats to watch for SEC play
description: As Texas heads into the eight week grinder of SEC play, Texas has some key areas to focus on.
fullText:
We are four games into the No. 1 Texas Longhorns' 2026 season, coming off of a bye week where Steve Sarkisian's program needed to get healthy and get aligned heading into the eight-week slog to close SEC play. Most of the year, the Longhorns have looked like a bit of a half team, with a championship-level defense carrying an offense that has flashes of brilliance but can't sustain its part when it matters. Texas has lofty goals for the year, hoping to compete for the SEC and national championships, but what should we watch as they head into the Red River Showdown and beyond?

Texas is perfectly average offensively on third downs through the first four games, which puts them firmly at No. 3 in the SEC, behind Georgia and LSU. However, it has been a case of diminishing returns for them over the first four games and floated by the 73.3-percent performance against Texas State to open the season. In the following weeks, they converted 56.3 percent, 41.2 percent, and an abysmal 25 percent (3-12) against Tennessee. In fact, against Tennessee, Texas went from the opening drive to the 2:43 mark of the third quarter without converting on a third down.

Most teams in the country struggle in third and long, but Texas has yet to convert a single one this year on nine attempts. That percentage doesn't get much better on third and medium (between five and eight yards) — the Longhorns are 9-of-25 in that range and were 1-of-7 against Tennessee. The silver lining there is that Texas is almost automatic from anything shorter than five yards, converting 18-of-25 (72 percent) from that range.

A big part of the issue has been quarterback Arch Manning's play on third down, looking far from the presumptive top-five pick many assumed he would become heading into the season. On the surface, his third-down performance has been good, completing 60 percent of his passes on an eight-yards-per-attempt pace, with four touchdowns, but once again, that number thrives because of the opener against Texas State. In Games 2, 3, and 4, Manning completed 55.5 percent of his passes at 4.5 yards per attempt with just one touchdown.

Over three weeks, aside from a few flashes of brilliance, Manning's play hasn't warranted the preseason acclaim and is becoming concerning as Texas heads to Dallas.

He currently sits ninth in the SEC in yards per game, wedged between Oklahoma's John Mateer and South Carolina's LaNorris Sellers, which may have been the company you expected him to keep in the SEC, but probably much closer to the top of the table. Manning came out of the gates hot, passing for 305 yards and four touchdowns against Texas State, but failed to crack 200 yards in the following two games and only beat that mark by one yard against Tennessee. Manning's seven touchdown passes are tied for No. 11 in the conference, thanks in large part to the four touchdowns he threw in the opener.

Post-Bobcats, he has thrown just three touchdowns and two interceptions and is averaging just 6.33 yards per drop back, which would put him just ahead of Marcel Reed for the worst average in the conference.

There was a lot made of the Longhorns' undisciplined play in Knoxville, with the glut of penalties and their inability to put together a sustained drive. But outside that one game, Texas has played more disciplined football than we've seen in years under Sarkisian. You can't say Tennessee wasn't a mess, nearly doubling their season totals in both penalties and penalty yardage in one outing. However, in their first away game in a hostile environment, it's hard to make a trend out of one week.

Hidden yardage and downs are where this shows up the most for Texas, losing 51 yards on offense while giving opponents 102 yards and eight free first downs due to penalties. What makes it worse is that three of those eight came on third downs, when Texas would have gotten off of the field otherwise.

Through the first three weeks, Texas was penalized just 14 times for just 135 yards – an average of just four penalties for 45 yards per game, which would put them second in the conference. If Texas's current average holds for the year, they will have improved from last year's performance, and Tennessee will be more of an outlier and less of a red flag.

title: OU football vs Texas TV channel, odds, scouting report for Red River Rivalry
description: Fresh off a bye week, Oklahoma heads to the Cotton Bowl to face No. 1 Texas on Saturday in Dallas. Here's everything you need to know about the game.
fullText:
NORMAN — Fresh off a bye week, Oklahoma is looking to flip the script on what's been a disappointing season thus far.

The Sooners, which sit at 2-2 after losses to Georgia and Michigan, now head to the Cotton Bowl to face No. 1 Texas (4-0) in the Red River Rivalry in Dallas.

OU has lost two consecutive games to the Longhorns and three of the last four in the series. From 2016-21, the Sooners won six of the seven contests but since coach Brent Venables took over OU is 1-3.

"It'll be a great challenge," Venables said on his coach's show last week. "It's something that we need to get on the right side of it, we haven't been on the right side of it. It's always an awesome atmosphere and a big deal to people on one side or the other of the Red River."

Texas defeated then-No. 1 Ohio State on Sept. 12 at home and then-No. 14 Tennessee on Sept. 26 on the road.

Venables is sticking with quarterback John Mateer for now even after he turned the ball over three times in the first half of the Sooners' road loss to the Bulldogs. This time last year, Mateer played against the Longhorns 17 days removed from surgery to repair a broken thumb.

If OU wants to compete with Texas, it'll have to limit its disastrous turnovers. In the Sooners' last three games, they've lost the turnover battle 9-2.

It'd certainly help OU if it was able to get back some injured players like safety Michael Boganowski, left tackle Michael Fasusi and linebackers Owen Heinecke and Cole Sullivan.

Here's everything you need to know about the 122nd edition of the Red River Rivalry:

Stream OU vs Texas live via ESPN

More: What's gone right, wrong for OU football through four games of 2026 season?

Best player: Texas third-year edge rusher Colin Simmons will be the best player on the field Saturday. The 6-foot-3 Dallas native recorded 5.5 sacks in the Longhorns' win over the Volunteers. No OU player has more than 2.5 sacks the entire season. Simmons is a projected top-10 pick in next year's NFL Draft and should feast against a struggling Sooners offensive line.

The case for Texas: As listed above, the Longhorns have two of the best wins in the nation. Quarterback Arch Manning has done enough with 862 passing yards with seven touchdowns and three interceptions. He also has perhaps the most explosive supporting cast in the country with former OU running back Hollywood Smothers and receivers Cam Coleman and Ryan Wingo. Texas' defense ranks eighth among Power Four teams in points allowed per game and will have a field day if the Sooners continue to turn the ball over at an alarming rate.

The case for OU: The Sooners' defense should give the Longhorns offense some issues. OU's unit is also one of the nation's best and will only improve if it can get healthier. The tallest task will be moving the ball on offense. If offensive coordinator Ben Arbuckle can show some of the things we saw in the Georgia game without Mateer's turnovers, OU will have a shot.

title: Texas QB Arch Manning’s uncle shares telling family standard ahead of draft decision
description: Eli Manning took the Arch Manning question on The Colin Cowherd Podcast, in an episode released on Thursday, Oct. 1, with his nephew four games into his second season as Texas’ starting quarterback. Eli skipped the timeline and described what the Mannings have always expected to get out of college, a standard the family’s own […] The post Texas QB Arch Manning’s uncle shares telling family standard ahead of draft decision appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
fullText:
Eli Manning took the Arch Manning question on The Colin Cowherd Podcast, in an episode released on Thursday, Oct. 1, with his nephew four games into his second season as Texas' starting quarterback. Eli skipped the timeline and described what the Mannings have always expected to get out of college, a standard the family's own history has already tested.

Arch redshirted as a freshman in 2023, so he is a redshirt junior this fall with the 2027 season still available. He can declare for the 2027 NFL Draft after this season or play one more year in Austin and enter the 2028 draft.

Peyton Manning faced a version of that choice after the 1996 season, when he was widely viewed as the likely No. 1 pick, and went back to Tennessee anyway. "I didn't want to be 50 years old wondering what my senior year in college would have been like," Peyton said. That December, he threw for 373 yards and four touchdowns as the Vols came back to beat Auburn 30-29 in the SEC Championship Game, and he went first overall in 1998.

Eli redshirted at Ole Miss and still started four seasons before going first overall in 2004. Archie Manning played out his eligibility at Ole Miss before going second overall in 1971. In 2025, Archie said Arch would not enter the 2026 draft, which held up when Arch returned for this season. Asked about Arch now, Eli described the same approach.

"Yeah, that's the whole point of college, to enjoy being in college, to get better every year. It's opportunities to play more games, to get better, to get more prepared for the NFL. To try to win a national championship or an SEC championship, to be a captain of the team. Like, all those things were important to us," Eli said on The Colin Cowherd Podcast.

"It's not just about, hey, this is all about getting through the NFL and going to the next step. No, it's about enjoying your experience, enjoying your teammates, becoming a better player, becoming a better leader, building something special with the guys that have all been there together. So I'm proud of Arch and how he's handled this and his mindset," Eli added.

Former New York Giants QB Eli Manning seemingly confirmed that his nephew and Texas Longhorns QB Arch Manning is at least considering returning to college for one more season and declaring for the NFL Draft in 2028.

Arch is currently going through his second season as the… pic.twitter.com/IvhvC0M6Vb

— NFL Rumors (@nflrums) October 3, 2026

Arch's first full season as the starter in 2025 produced a 9-3 regular season and a 41-27 bowl win over Michigan, but no SEC title. No Manning has won a national championship, and Peyton remains the only one with an SEC crown. Texas was 4-0 after its Sept. 26 win at Tennessee, so the chase Eli described is open right now.

Arch reportedly made $6.5 million in NIL money in 2024. His uncles played college football long before players could collect anything like it, so another year at Texas costs Arch far less than it would have cost them.

Eli never said which draft Arch will enter, and Arch has not announced anything. The decision waits on a season that is barely a month old.

title: San Diego State faces mumps outbreak before Texas State game: What we know
description: The San Diego State football team is dealing with a mumps outbreak ahead of Saturday's game against Texas State. Here's what to know about the illness.
fullText:
San Diego State football listed 33 players Thursday on its injury report, with 21 being either questionable, doubtful or out. While some are dealing with football-related injuries, at least 14 players have the mumps, with a 15th being a probable case, according to a university bulletin.

The San Diego Union-Tribune reported Sept. 18 that there were three confirmed and two probable cases of the illness. The Union-Tribune then reported Monday that four more SDSU players had been infected.

Texas State is slated to travel to San Diego for its first conference matchup as a Pac-12 program. Here's what to know about how the breakout affects the Texas State Bobcats' Saturday game against the Aztecs.

SDSU running backs Lucky Sutton and Javion Kinnard are out and doubtful, respectively, for Saturday's matchup after suffering injuries against Toledo. Guard Michael Levelle Watkins is out, while the entire tight end room is on the injury report. Head coach Sean Lewis declined to name the players affected by mumps when asked, citing federal privacy laws.

"The football gods have not really favored us with the injury luck," Lewis told reporters Wednesday.

Most recover from mumps within a week to 10 days, according to the Cleveland Clinic.

Dr. T. Ghosh, medical director of San Diego State Student Health Services, said in an email Wednesday that mumps symptoms can develop 12-25 days after exposure. Therefore, the number of players affected could grow by the time the Aztecs release the final injury report ahead of their game against the Bobcats.

The most apparent physical symptoms include puffy cheeks and a tender, swollen jaw. Fever, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, loss of appetite and pain or tenderness near the ears or jaw are other common attributes.

Mumps spreads through respiratory droplets. Sneezing, coughing, sharing utensils and even talking are ways mumps can spread throughout a group.

The SDSU website states that immunization requirements include two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, or laboratory evidence of immunity, subject to approved exemptions.

The Centers of Disease Control and Prevention website says that two vaccine doses are 97% effective against measles and 84% effective against mumps. Vaccinated people can still incur mumps for a variety of reasons, including prolonged exposure to someone with the virus or if an immune system's ability to fight the infection decreases over time.

title: Analytics experts weigh in on Colorado's upset chance vs. Texas Tech
description: Analytics experts are skeptical about Colorado's chances against No. 10 Texas Tech in this weekend's Big 12 matchup in Boulder.
fullText:
Colorado faces its toughest challenge of the season so far with the No. 10 Texas Tech Red Raiders coming to Boulder for a Saturday evening matchup.

After back-to-back losses, including dropping their Big 12 opener to Baylor, most people are down on the Buffs and rightfully so. The analytics community is especially concerned with the Buffaloes' past two performances.

ESPN's Bill Connelly listed Texas Tech as one of his top-15 teams on upset alert, but it didn't spark much confidence that Colorado could actually pull it off.

"The Buffaloes' defense has become far more aggressive and disruptive and can challenge a Tech offense that boasts strong efficiency numbers (15th in success rate) but doesn't make loads of big plays, turns the ball over too much and is dealing with O-line injuries...Only one half of the matchup is intriguing, however -- there's little reason to think the Buffaloes will actually score.. It will take serious Boulder magic for this to become interesting." - Connelly

Clearly, Connelly thinks it is at least a possibility that Colorado beats Texas, but nearly everything would have to go right.

Diving deeper into the analytics, SP+ projects the Red Raiders to win by 21 points while ESPN's Football Power Index has Texas Tech winning by 16.1 points. Based purely on the numbers, Colorado has little business being even close to Texas Tech, but as Connelly points out, the Buffs' defense versus the Red Raiders' offense is a matchup to exploit.

President Donald Trump warned Republicans that Texas and Michigan are among the states the party is “worried about” ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, while speaking to voters in Oklahoma on Thursday.

Fresh off an event in Texas, Trump told a crowd in the reliably Republican state that he was not concerned about Oklahoma but that Republicans needed to turn out voters in other states.

"I feel a little foolish, you know. I’m saying, 'go out and vote, go out and vote.' You’re gonna, they’re gonna win in the last half, but still go out and vote," Trump said. "But we’re not worried about them. We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states."

Trump later said Republicans need to get the word out about the midterms, citing what he described as 35 to 40 races that the party is concerned about.

"But we have to get the word out because we have to win in those 35. Maybe you could even say 40 places, 40 races," Trump said. "You have many, you have hundreds of races, but it’s all about 40."

Trump also again urged supporters to imagine that he himself was on the ballot.

"So you have to pretend I’m on the ticket and turn out for a midterm victory that’s really too big to rig," Trump said.

Trump sought to rally Republicans by attacking Democrats over inflation and immigration, repeating claims about the number and backgrounds of migrants who entered the country during the Biden administration.

Trump has repeatedly made claims about millions of migrants entering the U.S. from prisons and mental institutions, but those claims have been disputed and are not supported by evidence showing that foreign governments emptied prisons or institutions and sent those people to the United States.

The president also said his administration was running the country well but criticized Republicans for what he called poor "public relations."

ABC News' Jon Haworth contributed to this report.
