fullText:
The suspect was charged with felony terroristic threat against a public servant.

A man accused of plotting a "violent attack" on the Texas Capitol in Austin is in custody after state authorities say they received a tip about the alleged threat and worked through the night to track down a suspect.

The Texas State Department of Public Safety and the FBI thwarted a "credible threat" against the state capitol, according to a notice sent to Texas state senators Wednesday and reviewed by ABC News. The alleged attack was to occur on Thursday, according to the notice and Texas DPS.

Texas DPS said it learned of the threat Tuesday evening. Special agents worked alongside the FBI and local partners before arresting 40-year-old Benny Caldera Jr., whom it called the "main suspect," at his residence in Converse, Texas, at around 3 a.m. Wednesday.

Caldera was transported to the Bexar County jail and has been charged with felony terroristic threat against a public servant, according to Texas DPS.

According to an official briefed on the investigation, the suspect had allegedly been threatening to conduct a mass shooting at the Texas Capitol on Thursday and had been collecting ammo and had guns.

Authorities were notified by people who knew the man that he has been growing more angry and potentially violent recently, the official said. Neither Caldera nor his wife are cooperating with the probe at this point, the official said, but other family members and co-workers are talking to investigators.

In recent weeks, the suspect had voiced anger over the state and direction of the country and the Palestinian cause, among other things, the official said. He also allegedly had been doing drugs more heavily.

Investigators are working to obtain search warrants for the suspect's devices to determine if he had any accomplices or co-conspirators and what significance Thursday's date has, according to the official.

FBI Director Kash Patel commended the investigation, calling the work of Texas DPS "outstanding."

"Threaten Americans or our institutions and law enforcement will move FAST," he said in a post on social media.

In the notice to state senators, Texas State Senate Secretary Patsy Spaw said the alleged threat was not cause for concern but that she wanted to let members know about it.

"The investigation is ongoing, and there is and will continue to be an enhanced DPS presence at the Capitol," Spaw wrote in the notice.

title: White House removes CNN from press pool for Trump's upcoming trip to Texas and Oklahoma
description: President Donald Trump speaks to the media aboard Air Force One on its way to Joint Base Andrews, Md., from Ireland on Sept. 13.
fullText:
The White House on Wednesday removed CNN from the press pool that’s set to cover a trip by President Donald Trump on Thursday, escalating a feud with the cable network after a federal judge blocked the administration’s push to restrict its media access.

CNN had been designated to travel with Trump on Thursday, according to a press rotation document the White House released Sunday. But when the daily guidance came out for his scheduled visit to a truck manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas, followed by remarks in Durant, Oklahoma, it did not list CNN as providing pool coverage.

The move comes less than a week after a federal judge halted Trump’s effort to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. It also comes after the White House barred CNN from flying on Air Force One over the weekend when Trump traveled to Tennessee, when the network was scheduled to provide pool coverage. (The judge’s order was limited to media access on the White House grounds.)

Emily Kuhn, a spokesperson for CNN, confirmed the cable network’s removal from planned pool coverage but did not provide additional comment. Instead, she pointed to an earlier statement from Theodore Boutrous, an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico in their fight with the White House over press access.

“As we have said from the beginning, the President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process,” Boutrous said in a statement Monday, when the three news outlets asked a federal judge to extend his pause on Trump’s ban.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about CNN’s exclusion from Thursday’s trip.

The White House press pool is a group of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, each day’s designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public.

The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last week in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

Other member networks of the pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in pool duties last week in solidarity with CNN.

NBC News did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the exclusion of CNN for Thursday’s trip and whether it intended to take any action.

Trump has restricted access for other news outlets before. In 2025, he banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and certain events for not referring to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America — his preferred name for the gulf.

The AP sued, and the case continues.

title: On Texas' lack of offense, bad SEC refs and running steps for bad behavior | Bohls' nine things
description: The Texas offense remains inconsistent. The SEC refs had a bad game vs. Tennessee. And running steps for bad behavior. Kirk Bohls' nine things
fullText:
AUSTIN - While I got ya, here are nine things and one crazy prediction:

Anyone who has spotted the Texas offense, please call Bellmont Hall. It's been missing since the fourth quarter of the Ohio State game. It sure wasn't seen in Knoxville last Saturday. Steve Sarkisian praised Texas' offense for its fast start with a touchdown drive on its first series of the Tennessee game and for its next-to-last series with a game-sealing touchdown but didn't see a whole lot of continuity in between. The Longhorns now rank 83rd in offense nationally and an even worse 92nd in rushing as the defense carries this team. It's probably the worst a Texas offense has looked since Sarkisian's first season in 2021 when it went 5-7. He said Monday he doesn't anticipate making any changes in the starting lineup and didn't sound as if newly eligible Cole Hutson figures to get any playing time soon. … But one wonders when this inefficient offense catches up with Texas. When I asked if Texas can win a championship with this lackluster offense, he said, "I don't know because I don't know all the teams that we're going to play yet. What I do know is we need to play better offensively." Seems to me the problem remains the offensive line, all of whom got poor grades in run blocking from Pro Football Focus from between 54.3 (right guard Brandon Baker) and 63.2 (left tackle Trevor Goosby), but Arch Manning hasn't shown as much progress as expected. Sarkisian, however, disagreed and said he though Manning "played a pretty good game." … Manning still has accuracy issues, completing just 63.5% of his passes. Consider that 25 fellow quarterbacks are connecting on 70% or more of their throws, including Miami's Darian Mensah, who is 89% accurate and has thrown just 11 incompletions with 14 touchdowns and zero interceptions. Arch has seven touchdowns and three interceptions, one the bizarre ricochet off Cam Coleman. … Penalties also continue to be alarming. Texas ranks as the 90th worst team in that category after being whistled for 11 penalties for 115 yards on Saturday. Notre Dame, by point of comparison, ranks the most-disciplined team with only 10 penalties all year. The last two games alone, refs have stepped off 19 penalties for 203 yards. … Sarkisian said Texas needs to do better on first and second downs to minimize the third-and-long situations. Well, of course. But how? Eleven of the 30 called runs went for losses or no more than 1 yard. That's unacceptable. … Manning has to get the ball to Coleman than once a game. … I loved the ingenuity of the twin punt return set where Ryan Niblett ran to his right as a decoy for the Volunteers' punt coverage team but the ruse was foiled when Niblett waved for a fair catch and negated a long punt return by Jermaine Bishop Jr. … Sarkisian said injured running back Hollywood Smothers could have played in an "emergency," and should be healthy enough to play against OU on Oct. 10 after recovering from an ankle injury.

When it's illegal. Or should have been when Tennessee tried the ploy near the end of its 20-17 loss to Texas on Saturday. The officials blew it. The league office clarified that ruling Monday when it stated the Volunteers should have been flagged on the play, penalized 5 yards and made to re-kick. That kind of missed call that very well could have impacted the outcome of the game is inexcusable. The refs didn't know the rule. Quite frankly, I thought this was the worst officiating crew I've ever seen. I thought they were horrible from the outset when they ruled Texas was short of a first down on two third-and-1 attempts although it looked to me the Longhorn runner made it on each try. It took a ruling from the replay booth to learn Texas had successfully made the first down. I believe this crew should be suspended from doing SEC games for a minimum of one week. The league does not comment on crew's game assignments. … The SEC is off to an impressive 10-2 start against other Power 4 schools, the best in the nation. The Big Ten, meanwhile, is only 4-10 after winning the last three national championships. The ACC has a 6-9 mark, and the Big 12 5-7. … Sarkisian said he's not at all surprised by the strong starts of Florida and Mississippi State, to name two teams on his schedule. When a reporter said they weren't on many's dance card at the start of the season, Sarkisian said, "They were on my card. I tried to tell you guys about Florida last year. No one wanted to believe me. They've got real players in Gainesville, and they've kind of figured it out. This league is no joke." Funny how Texas fans were more worried about Oklahoma and Texas A&M during preseason than the Gators and Bulldogs. After OU, Texas' next five opponents are all ranked, giving the Longhorns the No. 2 toughest schedule. … Since the start of 2023, Texas has five road wins over ranked teams, more than any other team in college football. It also has 16 wins over Top 25 teams, six of them in the Top 10. It's also gone unnoticed that the Longhorns are 11-1 in their last 12 games with only a road loss to College Football Playoff-bound Georgia. That's pretty impressive. The Bulldogs are 13-1 in their last 14. Alabama is 7-3 in its last 10. Ohio State is 3-3 in its last six. Oregon is 11-3. Indiana, of course, leads all teams with a 20-game win streak.

The Texas baseball team, fresh off its first College World Series appearance under Jim Schlossnagle, has finished a month of practice and will play Houston at Dell Diamond on noon Saturday in an exhibition game. Texas will also move to Dell Diamond, the Disch-Falk batting cages and even Royal-Memorial Stadium for the remainder of its fall workouts. That's because the school is ripping up the turf at Disch-Falk and replacing it with a new FieldTurf that will be flatter and play a bit faster than its slower pace. Also, the dimensions in left field will move in 8 to 10 feet. "I would say the ballpark is definitely going to become more offensive because our turf is really the slowest that we play on all year, and you hit uphill and run uphill. You're going to have to be a better defender." … Shortstop Adrian Rodriguez, who hit for the cycle in Omaha, will give up switch-hitting and bat only from the left side as he continues his recovery from two hand procedures. Second baseman Ethan Mendoza is about to start swinging a bat after his summer shoulder surgery. … All-SEC closer Sam Cozart is probably going to transition to a starting role. Asked if any of the 23 new players were confused when they met the fully bearded and mustachioed Cozart, he said, "Yeah, a few of the younger ones thought I was a coach." Cozart has already become a leader. "Leading by example isn't really leading. So I lean toward vocal leadership. … I think for pretty much every freshman coming to college, especially to the University of Texas, this big of an atmosphere, you can be scared and so it's just getting them over the fear of being new? Was I scared? For about a week." He said winning a national title next summer brings "a major sense of urgency from the returners." … Schlossnagle is blown away by the maturity of freshman catcher Jax Robinson from Waxahachie. "Jax has frankly been the best hitter on the team this fall. Not just the best new hitter, but the best hitter on our team to this point.." He and fellow freshman Brady Murrietta of Yorba Linda, Calif., are competing with Saint Mary's transfer Ian Armstrong for the starting catcher position. … All-American Anthony Pack Jr. is the likely starting center fielder, a position last year's left fielder played for 10 games on the USA national team this summer without an error. He smacked 12 home runs last year but said Monday, "I still say I'm not a power hitter, to be honest. All my home runs came by accident."

Texas has pointed out that schools are not legally allowed to fine athletes like Colin Simmons for his vulgar celebration because they are technically not employees under labor law and there is no collective bargaining agreement because these athletes are unfairly not represented. So unless there is language stating moral clauses in Simmons' and his teammates' NIL contract, Texas doesn't have any financial recourse. … That doesn't mean Sarkisian can't punish his players in other ways like suspensions or punishments like getting Simmons and Raleek Brown up at 5 a.m. to run 500 stadium steps at DKR after their lewd celebrations. Better yet, I'd get the entire defense up that early every morning to run those steps with him. Call it team bonding. That's what Darrell Royal would have done. The Texas administration has chosen not to comment publicly on the issue. … It should be mentioned that no one is saying Simmons is a bad person. He moved his mother and 11-year-old autistic brother Clayton to Austin so he could receive better medical treatment. He's also held football camps for special needs kids and raised money through his foundation Clay's Color Crew for autism awareness. I just think he always plays with an edge, and his emotions got the better of him for the over-the-top celebration. I can't help but think of the days when Earl Campbell handed the ball to the ref after he scored touchdowns. … That wasn't the only shameful play of the week. I don't know what was worse, USC's Desman Stephens II's cheap shot on Oregon quarterback Dante Moore that sent him to the hospital or his celebration of the textbook targeting play afterward and the congratulations his fellow Trojans were showering on him. … On the other side, did you see Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss waiting until after Jon Sumrall's interview to hug and congratulate the Gators' coach? So classy. … Texas defensive tackle Hero Kanu was named a semifinalist for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy, the National Football Foundation announced. In its 37th year, the Campbell Trophy is a scholar-athlete award that annually recognizes an individual as the absolute best in the nation for his combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership.

It's always amusing to me how much hate mail I get over my Associated Press Top 25 ballot each week. This ain't Russia. We're not all going to pick our teams the same way. People love to shoot the messenger. And the criticism comes from the same haters who say the poll doesn't matter. So which is it? It's just entertainment, folks. I've often stated I have a very fluid ballot, especially in September, when teams are sorting themselves out. I've been very impressed with Wake Forest for its competitive loss to Miami and upset of Louisville and put the Demon Deacons at No. 17, one spot ahead of the Cardinals. The same goes for unbeaten UCLA at No. 20. I also bumped Iowa up five spots to 13th after beating Michigan. Ranking the final five of the Top 25 is the most difficult exercise of all. … As for keeping Texas No. 1, I still believe the Longhorns have the two best wins of the season over Ohio State and No. 14 Tennessee. However, I do struggle to understand ESPN's Football Power Index that has Ohio State at No. 3 and Texas at No. 4. If that's the case, why even play the game?

I think Kamario Taylor is the new favorite to win the Heisman now that Trinidad Chambliss fell to Florida. He could be the first to go from invisible to Heisman winner since Barry Sanders went from a kick returner to a star tailback at Oklahoma State. …  I think I love Justin Verlander's sweet, poignant goodbye in the final game of his career when his 7-year-old daughter, Genevieve, came to the mound to take him out and embraced her dad in a big hug. So touching. … I think karma has its way of evening things out. Right, Michigan? … I think Georgia is the most untested team in college football. The Bulldogs' schedule is ranked 123rd out of 136 teams. … I think Notre Dame might be second in the untested category. The Irish rank 99th nationally in plays from scrimmage of 10 yards or more. … I think Indiana can be had. Northwestern is much improved and gave the Hoosiers fits Friday night. … I think Lincoln Riley is an average coach. He did very little with Caleb Williams and not that much more with Jaiden Maiava. … I think Brent Venables, the ultimate good guy, could be the first coach to get a contract extension and a pink slip in the same year. Georgia covering the two-touchdown spread against OU was my lock of the week bet last Saturday. … I think it's very sad that former Texas forward Justice Carlton, now with the Houston women's basketball team, tore an ACL in her knee and will miss the season. … I think people are sleeping on Alabama's football team, as incredible as that sounds. The Tide catch Mississippi State next, one of four road games in its next six opponents.

Texas senior Farah O'Keefe has climbed to the No. 1 spot on the World Amateur Golf Ranking list after earning her sixth career victory as the co-medalist at the Jackson T. Stephens Cup. title: The Texas courtroom where toddlers face immigration judges
description: Migrant children as young as 2 are showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to try make their case to stay in the US and avoid deportation.
fullText:
In a Texas courtroom Monday, 25 migrant children lined the pews — a 6-year-old pretended to fly an airplane, a 3-year-old played with the mic, and a teen girl tried to make eye contact with a friend. The judge reminded everyone of what was at stake.

“I see you’re smiling and think these proceedings are funny, but I need you to pay attention,” the judge told the teen girl. “They could determine whether you remain in the country or are removed.”

Migrant children as young as 2 are showing up at immigration courts nationwide, many without attorneys, to make their case to stay in the US and avoid deportation.

Inside the immigration court in Harlingen, Texas, on Monday, caseworkers quietly explained to the minors who everyone was — from the interpreter and secretary to the judge in a black robe.

Most of the children, dressed formally with neatly styled hair, waited impatiently for the judge. Among the first to appear before the judge was a 13-year-old Honduran boy named Angel. He didn’t have an attorney.

Asked whether there was a reason he couldn’t return to Honduras, Angel told the judge, “My mom and almost my entire family are here. It’s too dangerous to go back.”

But that wasn’t enough for the judge, who told the boy he did not qualify for asylum. “Would you like to request voluntary departure, or should I issue a removal order?” The judge asked.

“I don’t know,” Angel replied before bursting into tears. He stared ahead stoically and continued to cry, eventually saying: “I have no one. I have nothing.”

“I understand, but based on your answers, US immigration laws are very strict,” the judge concluded, and gave Angel until the end of the month to appeal his deportation order.

Hundreds of unaccompanied migrant children who were detained trying to cross the southern border or whose families were picked up by Immigration and Customs Enforcement are being held in shelters operated by the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Refugee Resettlement, which is tasked with the care of unaccompanied migrant children.

Under President Donald Trump, they have been increasingly forced to navigate a complicated and accelerated immigration process with dwindling help after the administration ended a long-standing contract for legal services this summer — and as officials try to wrap their cases at an unprecedented pace.

Interviews with more than a dozen lawyers, advocates, and current and former administration officials, as well as a review of court documents and internal agency memos, paint a picture of an immigration system that’s constantly changing, often with little notice, and as a result, fueling confusion and placing immense pressure on vulnerable children facing deportation.

Children as young as 3 appeared in the Texas courtroom Monday, accompanied by their caseworkers.

Mateo, a 3-year-old in a blue jacket with neatly combed hair, was in court for an initial appearance. When called to the defense table, he tested the microphone, drawing laughter from some in the audience. As the judge spoke with Mateo’s attorney, who appeared remotely, the 3-year-old talked and played with the microphone.

The judge later asked a group of 15 minors without attorneys: “Is this your first time in immigration court?”

“Do any of you want voluntary departure?” the judge asked.

No one raised their hand. Another child stretched her hands playfully toward the sky.

A federal law that’s been in place for nearly two decades, the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act of 2008, is supposed to provide protections for unaccompanied migrant children, including screenings to check whether they’re victims of human trafficking or have a credible fear of persecution in their home country.

But advocates and attorneys tell CNN those protections are being undermined under the Trump administration. Children are contending with a fast-tracked immigration process, including abruptly rescheduled asylum interviews, sometimes with only a 24-hour notice — and increasingly without legal help.

Immigration hearings that used to be spread out over months are now happening within days or weeks. And internal procedures are frequently changing.

Relatives and guardians of children, meanwhile, are facing additional hurdles to try to have kids released to them, which the administration says is intended for additional vetting.

Daniel Gestal, deputy director of the children’s program at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said asylum interviews and immigration hearings for children have been sped up recently.

“We have seen that increase over the last couple months and supercharged over the last few weeks,” he said.

That matters for a child whose case may be especially complex. Like adults, children must also present evidence to back up their asylum claim, and there’s no requirement for them to have legal representation throughout the process.

“The 4-year-olds don’t know where they are and what’s going on. They may understand that they’re talking to a judge, and the judge asked them their name, but that’s the extent of their understanding,” an advocate who works with unaccompanied children told CNN.

“I’ve never witnessed so many removals and to see it happen with children who are standing there completely alone,” the advocate said.

While immigrant advocates and attorneys say the changes made by the Trump administration appear intended to quickly remove migrant children, Trump officials argue it’s for the benefit of the children to ensure they aren’t put in harm’s way — and to ensure rigorous vetting.

The Executive Office for Immigration Review, which oversees the US immigration court system, denied claims that cases are being fast-tracked.

A spokesperson for the office said in a statement to CNN that the agency “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and makes scheduling adjustments as needed to ensure cases do not languish.”

In a critical change in July, the Trump administration allowed a yearslong contract to lapse. The contract, valued at $200 million a year, was with the Acacia Center for Justice, which subcontracted with 100 legal service providers across the US. Together, they provided counsel to more than 20,000 unaccompanied migrant children, according to the center.

The contract to the Acacia Center for Justice funded know-your-rights presentations, legal screenings and legal representation, among other services. Historically, not all unaccompanied children have had attorneys, but under the contract, they all had legal orientations, consultations and referrals.

“Before, under our contract, it was mandatory to enter into representation if a child was moving forward to the pleading stage while in detention. You’d never have a child in detention being ordered removed without representation,” said Shaina Aber, executive director of the Acacia Center for Justice.

In early August, the Office of Refugee Resettlement awarded up to $20 million to the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, a nonprofit organization, to provide legal services through December 31. But in the weeks that followed, attorneys and advocates said in court declarations that the USCRI attorneys either weren’t present or didn’t speak up as kids faced the court. The declarations were submitted as part of an ongoing lawsuit challenging the administration’s initial attempt to terminate the contract.

In a statement to CNN, Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson Emily Hilliard cited the contract with the US Committee for Refugees and Immigrants as evidence of its commitment to provide legal services to children. “Under the Trump Administration, ORR remains committed to ensuring that every unaccompanied alien child has legal representation in immigration court,” she said.

“ORR will continue facilitating the ability of [unaccompanied alien children] in its custody to fully participate in immigration legal proceedings with representation by counsel, including hearings before EOIR immigration judges, who manage their own juvenile case dockets and schedules and make independent decisions on asylum claims under consideration,” she added.

USCRI did not respond to request for comment about claims that its attorneys were either not speaking up or not showing up at some immigration hearings.

On Monday, an attorney from USCRI watched silently as a virtual “friend of the court” for some of the children, including Angel, according to Lauren Fisher Flores, legal director at ProBar, which provides legal services to unaccompanied children across South Texas.

“In the 20 years I have been in this field, I have never seen the immigration court strip children of their right to seek safety and protection under the law,” said Flores, who attended Monday’s hearing. “We are witnessing the unraveling of due process protections that have been enshrined in our laws for decades. Children deserve better than a fast-track deportation system.”

While some attorneys have continued representing their existing clients, many can’t take on new or additional cases because of the loss in federal funding. Estrella del Paso, which works with unaccompanied minors in El Paso, Texas, closed its program after the expiration of the $200 million contract in late July. Thirteen of the 18 staff members who worked in the program were laid off, according to a court declaration submitted by Melissa Mari Lopez, executive director at Estrella del Paso.

In some courtrooms, immigration judges are requiring children to answer to the charges brought against them by the Department of Homeland Security that they should be removed.

“The kids who are unrepresented, they can’t read the form, much less figure out how to file it. And if they don’t put an asylum claim in, the judges are ordering their removal,” one of the advocates told CNN. “Fundamentally, that’s a complete violation of due process for a child. No one is asking a single question — who will you go to? Will you be safe?”

The lack of, or limited access to legal services, can also significantly impact a child’s asylum claim, which requires an interview with a US asylum officer. The interviews can take hours and dive into potentially traumatic events. In the absence of lawyers, kids go into the interviews alone.

Attorneys told CNN they first try to establish a rapport with a child and then help them understand what to expect in those interviews. Flores described sitting in an interview last month with a 3-year-old, who couldn’t fit in the chair and who subsequently ended up on the floor putting Band-Aids on the furniture and playing with dinosaurs while the asylum officer tried to ask the child questions.

In a September memo reviewed by CNN, ORR told shelters that “in the coming weeks” US Citizenship and Immigration Services would request virtual interviews with kids claiming asylum. The memo states that the attorney of record and/or legal service providers should be notified.

USCIS said in a statement to CNN that it receives lists of kids in custody from Health and Human Services and coordinates with the agency to schedule those with pending asylum applications for interviews — either in person or by video conference, “depending on which is the most expeditious.”

“Whether the face-to-face interview is conducted in person or by video conference, all UACs undergo the same rigorous vetting and security check process,” the statement said.

While attorneys and advocates concede there are parts of the immigration process, like asylum interviews, that were taking too long to get scheduled, the sudden changes and quick timelines place extra stress on children.

“The kids feel that pressure. The terror level of being deported — the reality of that happening soon — is causing anxiety and panic across the board also, which influences how you’re going to do at the interview,” said Laura Nally, program director of the Children’s Program at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights.

In August, there was an average of 1,883 migrant children in HHS custody, according to federal data, lower than in previous years.

ProBar, an organization that provides legal services to unaccompanied migrant children across 17 facilities in South Texas, had been a subcontractor with the Acacia Center for Justice. It continues to provide representation to the clients it already had, but access to other children is now limited.

In a court declaration, the organization cited the case of a 7-year-old who, in August, appeared before an immigration judge without an attorney and was ordered to voluntarily leave the US. The child was given 30 days.

ProBar set up a hotline for the first time called Dory, a reference to the fish in “Finding Nemo” that helps reunite father and son, as a way to serve as a resource to children in custody. It has received more than 200 calls since early August.

“You have some kids expressing emotions, others that are shut down,” said Katherine Beck, an attorney at ProBar. “It’s really, really challenging.” There are 14 staff members responding to the hotline who speak to children about their experience coming to the US, gather general information and provide guidance on the immigration process.

“What we can offer is a deep knowledge of the process,” Beck said.

Many kids are choosing to voluntarily leave the United States and go back to their home country, with the promise of a $3,000 stipend offered by the Department of Homeland Security if they do.

title: Federal prosecutors charge Venezuelan man shot by ICE agent with assaulting an officer
description:
Federal prosecutors in Texas have charged a Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent earlier this month with assaulting a federal officer, according to court documents unveiled Tuesday.
The prosecutors accused 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez of striking an ICE officer with his vehicle's side-view mirror as he drove away in an attempt to evade arrest. Garces Perez faces one count of assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer.
An agent from the Department of Homeland Security's Homeland Security Investigations laid out the allegations in an eight-page affidavit filed in support of a criminal complaint in the U.S.

title: Three ways Colorado football can upset No. 10 Texas Tech
description: Colorado hosts unbeaten No. 10 Texas Tech on Saturday. Here are three ways the Buffaloes can clean up their offense and pull off the upset.
fullText:
Colorado football will return to Folsom Field on Saturday with two straight losses and a difficult assignment against No. 12 Texas Tech. The Red Raiders are 4-0 and opened as a near two-touchdown road favorite.

Colorado has enough talent to make the game uncomfortable for Texas Tech, yet it will need cleaner work from an offense that has scored only 20 points in its last two games. The Buffaloes also need to settle their quarterback plan after they replaced Julian Lewis with Isaac Wilson during the Baylor loss.

Here are the clearest ways Colorado might be able to pull off an upset vs. the Red Raiders.

Colorado needs a clear direction at quarterback throughout the week. Wilson led a 95-yard touchdown drive at Baylor and completed a 17-yard scoring pass to Williams after entering at halftime.

Lewis remains a talented young passer, but the offense has struggled to find rhythm across the past two games. A full week of first-team preparation for one quarterback would give Brennan Marion a chance to tailor the plan and avoid another midgame change.

Joseph Williams has become Colorado's most dependable offensive weapon, leading the team with 361 yards and three touchdowns. He set career highs at Baylor with 11 catches for 127 yards and a touchdown.

Quanell Farrakhan Jr. added seven catches for 117 yards in Waco, showing Colorado can still generate production despite injuries to Danny Scudero Jr. and DeAndre Moore Jr. Kam Perry and Ernest Campbell give the offense more options if the staff builds the game plan around quick throws, intermediate routes and shots downfield.

Texas Tech's backfield is the starting point. J'Koby Williams has 285 yards and three touchdowns, while Cameron Dickey has 227 yards and four scores. The pair has combined for 512 rushing yards and seven touchdowns through four games.

Colorado linebackers will be without Tyler Martinez after his foot injury at Baylor. Liona Lefau, Gideon Lampron and the rest of the room must handle the workload against a Texas Tech offense that uses quarterback Thomas Castellanos in a wildcat package near the goal line and has already rushed for two touchdowns.

Colorado's upset path starts with a strong showing from the secondary and linebackers and by giving the receivers a chance in a game with almost no margin for error.

title: Texas Gov. Abbott declares disaster as diesel prices soar to average $5.86 a gallon
description:
Gov. Greg Abbott declared a statewide disaster on Monday over soaring diesel prices and a worsening fuel shortage created by wars abroad.
The 30-day disaster declaration, which can be extended indefinitely, allowed Abbott to lift some restrictions on commercial transportation, which he said will alleviate some of the elevated costs. Diesel fuel is used in farming and commercial shipping, so elevated fuel prices are passed through to consumers in the form of higher costs for goods at the grocery store. 
The declaration expands the use of dyed diesel on Texas roads, suspends Texas Low Emission Diesel rules to the limit the federal government authorizes and raises the allowable weight for fuel, agricultural and timber loads.

SFA football rolls to 63-14 win over Northeastern State

title: ABC’s broadcast audio issues during Texas-Tennessee unrelated to Trump or Secret Service, per report
description: It turns out that the intense static noise during ABC’s broadcast of Texas at Tennessee over the weekend may not have been related to President Donald Trump attending the SEC clash. Before the game, the broadcast’s main storyline focused on how the president and his Secret Service detail could affect communication signals between teams during the game.…
fullText:
It turns out that the intense static noise during ABC's broadcast of Texas at Tennessee over the weekend may not have been related to President Donald Trump attending the SEC clash.

Before the game, the broadcast's main storyline focused on how the president and his Secret Service detail could affect communication signals between teams during the game.

"As you'd expect, Secret Service with heightened security today," said announcer Chris Fowler. "Fans got here very early. Sometimes, when the President moves during a game, it can affect the communication [in] the coaches' headsets and the communication with players on the field."

Reporter Laura Rutledge, however, clarified that both teams cleared their radio signals with the Secret Service and were not expecting any trouble communicating from the upper box to the sideline. The coaches prepared hand signals in case they couldn't call plays to players on the field.

Right after Fowler and Rutledge set the table, game analyst Kirk Herbstreit was almost unintelligible due to the distracting amount of static that cut in when he spoke. Fowler apologized for Herbstreit's sound, and most viewers assumed it was related to the adjustments for Trump. The noise lasted the entire first half.

Right as Laura Rutledge explains Donald Trump’s presence leading to communication issues for Texas and Tennessee, the ABC audio becomes a mess.

Chris Fowler and Kirk Herbstreit try to deliver the play-by-play in a painful listen for ABC viewers. pic.twitter.com/DAESHVhS7u

— Awful Announcing (@awfulannouncing) September 26, 2026

However, according to The Athletic's Andrew Marchand, that was just an unfortunate coincidence.

"You would think, President Trump was there, there was a lot of talk about the Secret Service. It had nothing to do with that, I'm told," Marchand said on his podcast Monday. "Audio board in the truck had problems. That was just coincidental with the president being there, that wasn't the issue."

During last season's College Football Playoff, Indiana faced similar in-helmet communication issues at the Rose Bowl. The technical trouble affected Pat McAfee during his Field Pass alt-cast.

Perhaps the issue is more about the amount of communication equipment and broadcasting capacity involved in big-time football games these days than Trump or the Secret Service.

title: Texas softball starts fall ball Tuesday. How to watch Teagan Kavan, Katie Stewart
description: Teagan Kavan, Katie Stewart and new faces like Isa Torres start fall ball for Texas softball
fullText:
Sure, Texas softball doesn't officially start defense of its national championship until early February. But like most teams across the country, the Longhorns play an abbreviated schedule in the fall that helps solidify the pitching rotation, determine the lineup and lay the foundation for what head coach Mike White and his program hope is a third consecutive championship run.

Texas begins fall ball Tuesday against Murray State. Here are five things to know about the Longhorns' fall schedule:

After Texas kicks off its fall schedule by hosting Murray State Tuesday (6 p.m. at McCombs Field), the Longhorns will host four more games: Oct. 13 against Texas State, Oct. 20 against Temple College, Oct. 27 against McLennan Community College and Oct. 29 against UTSA.

Texas will visit Texas A&M for its final fall game Nov. 6 at 7 p.m. at Davis Diamond in College Station.

MORE: PHOTOS: Best images from Texas softball's Women's College World Series championship wins

Tickets to McCombs Field during the regular season often sell out, and all of the seats in the infield bleachers are not available expect through season tickets. But all fall ball home games at McCombs Field are free to the public, with seats in the infield and outfield available on a first-come, first-serve basis.

Outfielder Zoey Abdullah becomes third Texas Longhorns softball pledge for 2028

Texas must replace a handful of players from the 2026 team that went 53-12 and beat Texas Tech for the second consecutive season in the Women's College World Series finals. They include four-year starting right-fielder Ashton Maloney, record-setting catcher Reese Atwood, All-American second baseman Leighann Goode and versatile pitcher Citlaly Gutierrez.

Pitcher Teagan Kavan returns for her fourth season as arguably the greatest clutch pitcher in the college game. She became the first player to win consecutive WCWS Most Outstanding Player awards this past season after earning four complete-game wins in Oklahoma City as well as the save in the title-clinching 4-1 win over the Red Raiders.

Texas also welcomes back All-Americans in first baseman Katie Stewart and outfielder Kayden Henry as well as star infielder Vivi Martinez and sophomore pitcher/slugger Hannah Wells.

Texas will replace the holes in its roster with a seven-player high school recruiting class that ranks third in the nation by On3 and a three-player transfer class listed as No. 2 by D1 Softball.

Infielder Isa Torres and catcher Samantha Swan, former teammates at Georgetown High School, transferred in from Florida State and Arizona State, respectively. Both earned All-American honors last season, and both are expected to slide into starting roles for Texas.

Among the freshmen, infielder Annie Abdullah, infielder Mia Clemmer and pitcher Madi Doty all rank as consensus top 20 national recruits and look poised for an early impact.

title: John Fetterman accidentally calls himself a 'lifelong Republican' during an event
description: Senator John Fetterman, Democrat of Pennsylvania, speaks at the Texas Tribune Festival, in Austin, on Saturday.Photograph: Brian Cahn/Zuma Press...
fullText:
With speculation about whether he may defect from the Democratic party swirling around him, the US senator John Fetterman described himself seemingly unintentionally as a "lifelong Republican" during a fireside chat in Texas over the weekend.

Fetterman made the comment when someone listening to him speak with CBS News political correspondent Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival on Saturday asked the Pennsylvania senator why he had not become an independent.

"Because I'm a lifelong Republican," Fetterman replied. Garrett promptly corrected him by saying, "Democrat," as Fetterman raised a hand and shook his head in disbelief.

"That's a moment right there that's clippable, ladies and gentlemen," Garrett said amid laughter from the audience. "Go, go, go – internet, spin wildly! Wildly spin, internet!"

Fetterman then remarked, "Yeah – I guarantee you that's going to break through. That'll get … clipped – yeah. I'm a lifelong Democrat, though, and that's … the point."

Social and news media commenters quickly seized on video of Fetterman's gaffe, with more than one characterizing it as a Freudian slip.

Fetterman has drawn questions over his loyalty to the Democratic party after joining Republicans in opposing his party's efforts to end the US war with Iran as well as to cut off military aid to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza.

He also appeared in a video praising the Republican Pennsylvania US senator Dave McCormick at a convention held by the latter's party in Dallas on 9 September.

Fetterman – who was elected to the US Senate in 2022 – has denied that he intends to defect to the Republican party. He has said he would only abandon the Democrats if they became "the anti-Israel party".

"I'm not going to be a Republican," Fetterman told a reporter at the US Capitol in a video published online by C-Span on 15 September. "Why can't you guys just wait till the midterms? And if I turn a Republican, then I'll be a liar."

At the Texas Tribune Festival on Saturday, Fetterman expressed his belief that it was "entirely possible" for the Democratic party to clinch a majority in the Senate during the federal midterm elections in November, with Republicans being predicted to lose seats in Congress. But he declined to indicate with whom he may side if he ends up holding a tie-breaking vote on any given issue in the 100-seat Senate after the midterms.

"Let's revisit after the midterms, and let's see what happens – you know – if I happen to be 51," said Fetterman, who was elected to the US Senate in 2022. "I don't know."

title: GoFundMe that raised nearly $290,000 for Texas couple pulled over 'factual' issues
description:
Donald and Josephine Johnson's GoFundMe campaign aimed to raise money for Josephine's cancer treatment. (KXAS)
GoFundMe pulled the plug Sunday on a campaign to raise money for an elderly Texas couple, saying it had “identified factual misrepresentations.” 
The account was created after the husband went viral for working a backbreaking job to cover his wife’s mounting bills for cancer treatment.
The digital fundraising site did not immediately reveal what kind of misrepresentations were behind its decision to end the campaign set to benefit Donald and Josephine Johnson.
The GoFundMe gained national attention and raised nearly $290,000 before it was pulled down.
fullText:
GoFundMe pulled the plug Sunday on a campaign to raise money for an elderly Texas couple, saying it had “identified factual misrepresentations.”

The account was created after the husband went viral for working a backbreaking job to cover his wife’s mounting bills for cancer treatment.

The digital fundraising site did not immediately reveal what kind of misrepresentations were behind its decision to end the campaign set to benefit Donald and Josephine Johnson.

The GoFundMe gained national attention and raised nearly $290,000 before it was pulled down.

The campaign was started by a “concerned stranger” identified as “Erin H,” who said she spotted on her Ring camera the 81-year-old husband struggling to carry heavy luggage up a flight of stairs.

The organizer said she asked why he was working such a physically demanding job at his age, and Johnson said his wife was fighting cancer and this was the only job he could find to pay the overwhelming hospital bills.

But somewhere along the line, GoFundMe said it found “misrepresentations” in the campaign.

The platform received a tip that the organizer of the campaign might not be who they said they were. GoFundMe investigators called the organizer, who admitted that she was in fact the Johnsons’ daughter, that she had shot the viral video and that the concerned stranger was a made-up persona.

The organizer, however, said the other aspects of Donald and Josephine Johnson’s story were true. She told GoFundMe’s team that the story would be more compelling if it were told by a stranger and not a family member.

“Our Trust & Safety team identified factual misrepresentations, which directly violates our Terms of Service,” the platform said in a statement to NBC News on Sunday. “As a result, the fundraiser has been removed and all donors have been refunded.”

The platform, which did not name the organizer of the fundraiser, said it has no choice but to take tough action in order to maintain trust with donors.

“Ensuring GoFundMe is a safe and trusted place to give and receive help is our top priority. Taking action like this allows GoFundMe to protect donors’ generosity and our continued ability to support people who are fundraising to help others,” GoFundMe said.

“GoFundMe’s policies, along with those of our payment processors, require authenticity and transparency for donors, and are strictly enforced,” it said. “Because that standard wasn’t met here, donors were protected under our GoFundMe Giving Guarantee, which guarantees a full refund in the rare case something isn’t right.”

The Johnsons’ appeal for help has since been taken to an alternate fundraising site, GiveSendGo.

There, the couple’s daughter, Amy Johnson, explained that her parents are fighting their mother’s pancreatic cancer and that the luggage-hauling job is real.

“My dad is 81 and still works delivering luggage so they can stay afloat,” according to the GiveSendGo listing. “The neighbor story is real. The doorcam video is real. The diagnosis is real. The job is real.”

A fundraising effort was already on for her dad via GoFundMe, but once the viral video emerged, the family decided to change the campaign’s organizer’s name to “Erin H,” to reflect the video captured by this stranger who wanted to remain anonymous, Amy Johnson said.

But that name change amounted to an unintentional violation of GoFundMe terms, according to the daughter.

“That was it. We didn’t know it was a problem,” the daughter said in a TikTok video. “I have to come out because someone wanted to do something out of pure kindness but wanted to remain anonymous.”

Amy Johnson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Donald Johnson could not immediately be reached.

GiveSendGo calls itself a faith-based platform that hopes to “share God’s love” in the most efficient manner possible. It has been used to raise funds for Kenosha, Wisconsin, shooter Kyle Rittenhouse and a Minnesota woman caught using a racist slur on camera and to support Canadian truckers who blocked highways in protest of Covid restrictions.

Asked about the validity of the Johnson campaign, GiveSendGo said in a statement: “We do not allow fundraisers to deceive the public about who or what is being fundraised for. Every fundraiser on GiveSendGo is reviewed by our verification team before any funds are released.”

title: ‘Watch Yo Mouth’: Colin Simmons Fires Back at CBS Analyst Over Peeing Penalty
description: Colin Simmons fired back, telling Brian Jones to "watch yo mouth," after he criticized Simmons' peeing celebration. fullText:
After CBS college football analyst Brian Jones criticized Colin Simmons' controversial peeing gesture in the Texas vs Tennessee game, Simmons fired back on Instagram, telling the analyst to "watch yo mouth."

Simmons drew an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty with 5:08 remaining in the second quarter of the Texas vs Tennessee game on September 26. Referee Rod Tucker announced the penalty — which quickly went viral — as being for "simulating using the restroom."

CBS Sports posted a clip of Brian Jones' analysis of Simmons on Instagram after the Texas vs Tennessee game.

Jones said about Simmons' peeing gesture: "How dumb do you have to be? You get off the field. It's 4th & 29. Yet they get a first down because of that personal foul… It's crude, it's classless, and it's vulgar. And it's not how a number one team or any team should behave."

Simmons replied with his verified Instagram account, writing: "watch yo mouth gang ion even kno who you is keep talking down on yo own color #sucka."

Heavy checked the source of Simmons' reply, and confirmed it did go back to Simmons' verified Instagram account.

Jones is is a former Longhorns player himself, who also played in the NFL for six seasons. He's now a well-regarded analyst on College Football Today.

Simmons and Jones were referencing a personal foul penalty that Simmons incurred after he sacked Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon. Following the sack, Simmons stood over Brandon and pretended to urinate on the field.

ESPN's Kirk Herbstreit called the celebration "idiotic" during the broadcast. The penalty extended Tennessee's drive instead of forcing a punt.

The comment came after Simmons made a separate post on Instagram, where he shared a screenshot from X apologizing for his actions. He shared in the Instagram story and on X: "All Glory to God 🙏 Thank you for listening to my prayers and forgive me for my actions. ♥️#5piece."

All Glory To God 🙏🏾 Thank you for listening to my prayers and forgive me for my actions. ❤️ #5piece

— Colin Simmons ☝🏾 (@ColinSimmons__) September 26, 2026

He also apologized in the post-game press conference, saying: "I do want to say I apologize for the celebration. I was definitely in the mode feeling myself. But it happens, charge it to the game."

Colin Simmons addresses his unsportsmanlike conduct penalty and apologizes for his viral celebration against Tennessee.

(via @EvanVieth) pic.twitter.com/tL8mgYzKsW

— FOX College Football (@CFBONFOX) September 26, 2026

“We took him out and we addressed it. I’m not gonna give the guy a death penalty for an unsportsmanlike conduct. It has to about the team and not the look at me.”

Steve Sarkisian on Colin Simmons’ unsportsmanlike penalty call. pic.twitter.com/ZgQV7mlEst

— Eric C. Henry (@EricCHenry_) September 26, 2026

In his post-game press conference, head coach Steve Sarkisian said: "We took him out, we addressed it, and put him back in. At that point, I'm not going to give the guy a death penalty, right, over an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty. We got to fix it, though. That can't continue as we move forward. As I touched on with the team in the locker room, we'll address that on Monday. What that looks like and how to control our emotions in the best way. I know guys are excited when they're making plays; the best thing you can do is celebrate with a teammate."

Meanwhile, fans had mixed reactions to Simmons' reply to Jones on Instagram. Some people supported Simmons, writing things like "keep that swagger big dawg" and "keep doing your thang man."

In a Reddit thread about the reply, college football fans were critical of Simmons' post. One person wrote, "For the record, Colin Simmons majors in Communication & Leadership at the University of Texas at Austin."

Another person wrote on Reddit, "This dude gonna drop to the second round."

Another joked, "My god he's doing everything he can to drop to the Eagles in the draft."

title: Former Texas A&M stars De’Von Achane, Mike Evans hurt in Week 3
description: Miami awaits more information on Achane’s knee, while Evans will be evaluated after leaving San Francisco’s win with a rib injury.
fullText:
Two former Texas A&M playmakers left their NFL games with injuries Sunday. Miami Dolphins running back De'Von Achane suffered a knee injury against the Kansas City Chiefs, while San Francisco 49ers receiver Mike Evans injured his ribs against the Arizona Cardinals. Neither returned.

Achane was involved in four of Miami's first five offensive plays before getting hurt on an 11-yard run in the first quarter. He walked to the sideline under his own power, but the Dolphins later ruled him out of their 24-10 loss. Miami had not determined the severity of the injury after the game.

Coach Jeff Hafley said the team was still gathering information and expected to know more Monday. His initial assessment was concerning

"It does not sound optimistic at this moment."

Hafley did not give a diagnosis or a timetable for Achane's return.

Evans entered San Francisco's game questionable with a hip injury but was cleared to play. He caught a 23-yard touchdown pass before suffering a separate injury in the second quarter. The 49ers ruled him out after halftime, then went on to beat Arizona 36-30.

NFL Network reported that Evans has a rib strain and will undergo a full evaluation Monday. After the game, 49ers coach Kyle Shanahan said the team was still determining whether the injury involved a rib or an oblique muscle. He did not estimate how much time Evans might miss.

For now, both teams are waiting on further medical evaluations. Achane's injury is the more worrying of the two based on his coach's comments, but it is too early to assign either former Aggie a return date.

title: Sen. John Fetterman says it's 'entirely possible' Democrats take back Senate
description:
Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania said Saturday that it's "entirely possible" his party could win control of the Senate in the midterm elections, but he also left the door open on his own political future. 
"Let's revisit after the midterm," Fetterman told CBS News' Major Garrett at the Texas Tribune Festival in Austin.
Democrats faced an uphill battle heading into the midterm cycle as they sought control the upper chamber, with 53 Republicans currently in the Senate and a map that appeared more favorable to the GOP. Despite Colin Simmons having five sacks for the Texas Longhorns, Arch Manning being interviewed over him has caused quite the controversy.

Simmons' five sacks, along with his lewd celebration that earned one of the most controversial and talked-about penalties in quite some time, became a huge talking point.

Emmanuel Acho took to X after seeing Fox Sports correspondents approach Texas Longhorns QB Arch Manning for an interview after their win over the Tennessee Volunteers.

Acho suggested that Manning was being interviewed despite an unremarkable performance and having very little insight to offer. He added that Colin Simmons deserved to be interviewed after being the team's standout performer.

"I can't wait for football coverage to evolve. We should be interviewing Colin Simmons post-game, the player who recorded 5 sacks & one of the most controversial penalties in recent history.

Arch Manning didn't do much against the Volunteers, with zero touchdowns while throwing for 201 yards and having one pass intercepted.

On the other hand, Simmons had an excellent game with eight total tackles, with six solo tackles and five sacks against the Volunteers.

The insinuation from Acho is that Manning, as one of the biggest names in college football, is being prioritised over players who outperformed him in the win.

Of course, many fans know that Arch is the son of Cooper Manning, the older brother of legendary NFL quarterbacks Peyton and Eli Manning.

Arch was also named after his grandfather and the patriarch of the Manning family, Archie Manning, another legendary quarterback who played for Ole Miss, the Houston Oilers, and the Minnesota Vikings.

As potentially the first third-generation quarterback in NFL history, Manning is a massive media figure and a huge name in college football.

And sometimes, that can lead broadcasters and media outlets to focus on him over the rest of his teammates, even when he hasn't played very well.

title: Texas vs Tennessee report card: Arch Manning, offense struggle; defense shines in SEC win
description: How the Texas Longhorns graded out in their 20-17 win over Tennessee. QB Arch Manning and the offense struggle, but Colin Simmons and defense gets high marks
fullText:
Considering the wild ending, Texas football won't soon forget its first trip to Rocky Top.

The No. 1 Longhorns (4-0, 1-0 SEC) opened conference play with a 20-17 win over No. 14 Tennessee (3-1, 0-1) at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville, Tenn. But the victory came with plenty of anxiety considering the Volunteers scored a touchdown with 1 minute, 22 seconds left in the game and recovered the subsequent onside kick.

But Texas held on for the win and now gets a week break before its annual grudge match Oct 10 against Oklahoma in the Cotton Bowl in Dallas.

Here's how the Longhorns graded out in a 20-17 win over Tennessee.

Arch Manning was more efficient than explosive with 201 yards on 14-of-19 passing. But he didn't toss a touchdown for the first time in the past 10 games and he threw up a prayer to a double-covered Cam Coleman that resulted in an interception. He also absorbed six sacks while failing to get rid of the ball despite decent pass protection. His legs didn't lead to any big plays, but they did lead to two flags for an illegal forward pass.

Hollywood Smothers landed on the injury report all week and missed the game with an undisclosed injury. That meant Raleek Brown carried the load with 67 yards and two touchdowns on 17 carries. Freshman Derrek Cooper had the other seven carries by Texas running backs but tallied just seven yards.

Veteran Ryan Wingo emerged as Manning's most reliable target with six catches for 74 yards. Freshman Jermaine Bishop Jr., the slight but speedy five-star recruit, continues to make more and more of an impact; he had two catches for 34 yards. But where was Cam Coleman? The high-paid portal arrival had just one catch and missed some possessions with an unknown injury.

Sure, Manning holds the ball a long time in the pocket. But the Longhorns did allow a season-high six sacks against a talented Tennessee front. And the line didn't get much push against a questionable Tennessee run defense; the Longhorns averaged just 1.7 yards a carry and totaled 262 yards.

This would have been an A+, but edge rusher Colin Simmons gets docked for his tasteless sack celebration that resulted in a 15-yard penalty and kept a Tennessee drive alive. But Simmons had reasons to celebrate since he tied a school record with five sacks and Texas racked up a total of 10 sacks, which ranks second on the single-game school record list. Tackles Hero Kanu (four tackles, one sack) and Maraad Watson (five tackles, one sack) dominated inside, and end Lance Jackson may just be the most well-rounded defensive lineman on the roster.

Rasheem Biles, a Pittsburgh transfer, continues to make his claim on more All-American honors after a team-high 13 tackles and a late sack that helped seal the win. Justin Cryer (nine tackles) remains a superb sidekick, but the unit does lack depth. Both Biles and Cryer rarely left the field while helping hold Tennessee to 221 yards of offense.

Tennessee quarterback Faizon Brandon picked on Texas cornerback Bo Mascoe a little bit, drawing two pass interference calls and the late touchdown pass to Mike Matthews. Brandon completed 17 of 29 passes for 145 yards, and the Vols became the first team this season not to turn the ball over against Texas. Texas slot corner Graceson Littleton continues to impress.

Yes, kicker Gianni Spetic made both of his field goals. But those were the only bright spots for a unit that gave up a punt return for a touchdown for the first time in 13 years and failed to cover an onside kick late in the game that could have cost Texas the win. The Longhorns also had an odd illegal fair catch call on Ryan Niblett that wiped out a good return by Bishop.

Defensively, coordinator Will Muschamp produced a brilliant game plan that suffocated a potent Tennessee ground game, which had just 70 yards on 44 carries. Credit head coach and play-caller Steve Sarkisian for sticking with the ground game, but the Longhorns had too many penalties. Texas endured season-highs with 11 penalties for 115 yards, and that ultimately reflects on the coaching staff.

title: Steve Sarkisian blames "society" for Colin Simmons's bizarre unsportsmanlike conduct foul
description: To cap a week in which the NFL went overboard with fines, Texas defensive end Colin Simmons did something that possibly would have gotten him banned for life by 345 Park Avenue.
fullText:
To cap a week in which the NFL went overboard with fines, Texas defensive end Colin Simmons did something that possibly would have gotten him banned for life by 345 Park Avenue.

After one of his Longhorn record-tying five sacks against Tennessee, Simmons celebrated by pretending to urinate on the field.

He seemed surprised when the officials penalized the move, with the eventual explanation being that Simmons was "simulating using the restroom."

Coach Steve Sarkisian addressed the situation following the 20-17 win.

"We took him out," Sarkisian said, via Tyler Lauletta of Awful Announcing, regarding the fact that Simmons, well, took it out. "We addressed it, and put him back in. I'm not gonna give the guy the death penalty over an unsportsmanlike conduct penalty. We've got to fix it though. That can't continue as we move forward."

That part is reasonable and appropriate. Then, things got a little screwy from Sarkisian.

"Unfortunately, in our society right now, we live in the 'look at me' society," Sarkisian said. "All of you guys have your Twitter accounts, and as fast as you can type something because you want everyone to look at your account, and you get clicks. Well, that's the world that we live in. So we've got to get to —it's about the team and focus on the team, and not so much 'look at me.' So we'll try to improve upon that, but five sacks was pretty cool today too."

Steve, don't simulate using the restroom on our leg and tell us it's raining. Society didn't lead Simmons to do something we've never seen a player do, because 99.999999 percent of all players know not to do it.

Still, we'd love to hear how Sarkisian would explain a similarly perverse celebration that was not penalized. Almost as much as we'd love to hear the explanation of the foul.

Well, in their quest to aid major-league history and prevent a sub-.500 team from winning their division, the Texas Rangers knocked the Twins around in a rain-delayed, 6-2 victory on Saturday afternoon. With the Houston Astros just underway, the Rangers improve to 80-81, and give themselves a fighting chance of claiming the West with another win tomorrow afternoon; if they do, they will at least guarantee that their ticket to the playoffs will come on the back of an even record.

For the first time since 2009, the Rangers hit four doubles in the same inning, a four-run second that summed up most of Bailey Ober's day. Nicky Lopez, Evan Carter, Alejandro Osuna, and Brandon Nimmo each had a two-bagger in the inning, which saw Ober give up four of his six earned runs, and five of his ten hits — all with two outs in the inning and nobody aboard.

It closed the book on Ober for 2026, leaving him with a 7-7 record and 4.47 ERA. He added five strikeouts and one walk to his final marks.

The Twins were not as successful in getting to Texas starter Nathan Eovaldi, who did not make it through five frames after tossing 71 pitches and booking it. Luke Keaschall doubled and scored in the first, but only three other Twins would tag Eovaldi for a hit, and the only other Twins run came after the white-hot Keaschall tripled and scored on a Josh Bell single in the bottom of the eighth.

The book is nearly closed on all the members of the Twins roster, with Dean Kremer scheduled to start Game 162 and finish off this season for good. Minnesota currently sits at 76-85, dead even with the Detroit Tigers; a win and a Tiger loss tomorrow would leave the Twins alone in third place to end the season.

fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A Texas city council candidate was arrested Saturday morning on a misdemeanor charge for "riot participation" in connection with behavior authorities said they observed at a protest against the shooting of a Venezuelan man by a federal immigration officer.

Texas Department of Public Safety troopers and special agents took Misael Ramos, 40, into custody around 8:45 a.m. Saturday on an outstanding warrant "stemming from his actions" during a Sunday protest, the agency's media department wrote in an unsigned email. Protesters on Sunday had been demonstrating against the shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin.

Ramos, who is running for city council in Austin, "was captured on camera taking construction barricades, sandbags, and other items and attempting to obstruct traffic," the department said. The department also provided photos and video it said captured "some of Ramos' actions" at the scene.

Ramos, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, denies any wrongdoing and will contest the charge, his campaign said in a news release.

"I didn't see any riots," said Ramos' attorney, Edmund "Skip" Davis. "I saw people out there chanting and protesting."

Ramos was released from custody during a news conference outside the county jail Saturday, with the crowd erupting in cheers. Ramos thanked those for being there, saying it was "one of the craziest mornings I have had in a long time." He spoke of his surprise arrest and criticized federal immigration raids in the community.

"When we fight," he said, to which those gathered replied, "we win!"

Garces Perez was shot Sunday and then taken to a detention center after an encounter with an immigration officer. An attorney for Garces Perez has said he was an asylum seeker and had a valid work permit.

"Like the hundreds of Austinites who were shocked to hear news that an ICE officer shot someone in the back, Misael quickly joined people at the scene of the incident to offer his condemnation of the incident and show solidarity by holding the line in the protest, chanting, and amplifying the incident through campaign channels," Ramos' campaign manager, Jeffrey Clemmons, said in a statement.

Kristen Dark, a spokeswoman for the Travis County Sheriff's Office, confirmed in an email that Ramos was booked into the agency's custody around 9:30 Saturday morning on a charge of riot participation.

Garces Perez was making a DoorDash delivery Sunday afternoon when ICE officers in an unmarked truck sideswiped his car twice, his attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch has said. He was shot and taken to a hospital, then released into ICE custody with a bullet still in his back, she said.

ICE and DHS haven't said what led to the shooting beyond that Garces Perez was "the subject of a targeted vehicle stop."

fullText:
KNOXVILLE – Rapid reaction from 13th-ranked Tennessee's 20-17 loss to top-ranked Texas before a checkered crowd at Neyland Stadium:

-In a stunning late sequence, Tennessee nearly overcame a 10-point deficit in the final 90 seconds. The Vols recovered an onside kick after scoring their first offensive touchdown with 1:22 remaining, but they weren't able to turn it into points. Faizon Brandon's Hail Mary pass fell incomplete in the end zone on the final play.

-Ultimately, strong defense and a punt-return touchdown weren't enough for Tennessee to overcome its inability to block Texas' defensive front. The Vols' offensive line was pushed around all game, resulting in a whopping 10 sacks, a lack of explosive plays and a quiet day on the ground. That last one was especially surprising, since Tennessee entered this game with one of the nation's best rushing attacks. Prior to that desperation TD drive by Tennessee's offense in the final minutes, it was averaging 1.5 yards per carry and 2.2 yards per play.

-Texas quarterback Arch Manning only threw 19 passes, but he completed 14 for 201 yards against an aggressive Tennessee defense that pressured him into six sacks and held the Longhorns' offense in check for much for this game. Manning did enough, though. With a 13-10 lead in the fourth quarter, he led an eight-play touchdown drive that ended up being the game-winning points.

-Brandon, the Vols' freshman quarterback, returned from a scary-looking injury in the first half to finish the game, though he appeared to be in pain during the final drive. After Brandon fell onto his right shoulder early while being tackled, sophomore backup George MacIntyre entered the game and threw three passes, completing one for 6 yards. Meanwhile, Brandon exited the injury tent and began throwing passes on the sideline before returning the game. The first play on his return? A quarterback run up the middle.

-Texas edge rusher Colin Simmons was a menace all game for Tennessee's offense, finishing with five sacks. Simmons, however, was also flagged for one of the dumbest, yet hilarious, penalties you'll ever see in the second quarter. After a sack of Brandon on third-and-13, which would've forced Tennessee to punt at its own 12-yard-line, Simmons instead gifted the Vols a first down when he celebrated by pretending to unzip his pants and urinate on the field. He was penalized for unsportsmanlike conduct, allowing the Vols to continue what ended up being a 15-play drive before it stalled without points at the Longhorns' 34.

After Qua Moss' punt return tied the game 10-10 in the third quarter, Texas replied with a 48-yard drive for a field goal to retake the lead. The key play was a 30-yard throw to Cam Coleman in which Manning withstood pressure (roughing the passer was called) to complete a pivotal pass on second-and-10, anyway, beating Ty Redmond in coverage.

1 – Number of offensive plays for Tennessee that gained 20 yards or more. And that was Brandon's TD throw to Mike Matthews in the game's final minutes. The longest gain of the first half was a 13-yard run, and the longest gain of the third quarter was an 18-yard pass.

This Tennessee defense might be for real. After allowing Texas' too-easy TD drive to open the game, Jim Knowles' unit responded and kept the Vols in this game all afternoon despite the offense's struggles. Manning rarely looked comfortable. He rarely had room to scramble, and the talented Longhorns couldn't get much going on the ground.

You expected that there would be freshman moments for Brandon. But this was an alarming afternoon for Tennessee's entire offense, and especially an O-Line that was exposed by the Longhorns' defensive front. Before, during and after Brandon's injury, it felt like nothing came easy for the Vols' offensively. Josh Heupel's teams won't often win big games when that's happening.

fullText:
James Talarico’s poll lead over Ken Paxton in the crunch Texas Senate battle has fallen by one point according to two new opinion polls, which also showed the number of undecided Texan voters has been reduced.

Democrats are hoping to win control of the Senate at the November midterms and victory in Texas—a traditional Republican stronghold that last elected a Democratic senator in 1988—would significantly boost their chances.

Friday saw the publication of the latest Texas Public Opinion Research survey which polled 1,007 likely Texan voters between September 19 and 22. The poll, which had a 3.6 percent margin of error, found state Representative Talarico leading current Texas Attorney General Paxton by five points with 49 percent of the vote against 44 percent.

The last Texas Public Opinion Research survey, of 1,000 likely Texas voters conducted from August 21-24, gave Talarico a six-point lead, with 48 percent of the vote against Paxton’s 42 percent.

Notably the proportion of undecided voters has also fallen from seven percent in August to three percent this month, with Libertarian candidate Ted Brown also gaining two percentage points. However, the decrease in Talarico’s support remains within the margin of error.

Separately a new Texas Southern University survey gave Talarico a lead of just one point, with 47 percent of the vote against 46 percent for Paxton and three percent for Brown. This survey of 1,800 Texan likely voters took place between September 15 and 19 and has a 2.31 percent margin of error.

Newsweek contacted the Talarico and Paxton senate campaigns for comment via email on Saturday outside of regular office hours.

Talarico leads Paxton according to eight different pollsters, though several are within the margin of error, and thus too close to call.

An Emerson College survey, conducted September 12-14, gave Talarico a 1-point lead with 47 percent of the vote to Paxton's 46 percent. The poll surveyed 1,000 voters with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Between August 30 and September 1, AARP surveyed 895 likely voters, giving Talarico a 4-point lead with a 3.3-point margin of error. Similarly, a YouGov/Univision poll of 1,000 registered voters that took place between August 27 and September 4 put Talarico ahead by 5 points, with a 3.6-point margin of error.
