fullText:
United States President Donald Trump is set to attend Saturday afternoon's showdown between the Tennessee Volunteers and the Texas Longhorns in Knoxville. It's widely known that the president's attendance at any public event causes a lot of logistical challenges, but it's safe to say that not many people knew about how Trump's appearance could directly impact the game itself.

As the Longhorns prepare for the road showdown with Tennessee, Texas head coach Steve Sarkisian gave some rather unique insight into one of the challenges that come along with Trump attending games, and the sports media world was stunned by his revelations.

During his Thursday press conference, Sarkisian revealed that this actually is not the first time that he will be involved in a game that Trump has attended. Sarkisian was the offensive coordinator at Alabama under Nick Saban when Trump attended the College Football Playoff National Championship following the 2017 season.

Given this experience, Sarkisian has some unique insight that he was able to share.

Sarkisian revealed that whenever the president moves throughout the stadium, all communication throughout the stadium has to be shut down, including the communication between the coordinators in the booth and the sideline as well as the in-helmet comms for the players.

"One thing we have to be aware of is when the President goes to a game, any time he enters, leaves or changes locations within the stadium, they cut all communication," Sarkisian said during his Thursday Zoom press availability, via 247Sports. "They cut all communication, so they cut your headsets to coaches and they cut headsets with coach-to-player communication."

Sarkisian added that this can happen without any warning, even for something simple like the president using the restroom.

"So, you have to have a plan for that, if and or when it happens and you don't get any warning," Sarkisian said. "It just cuts out. So, you have to have a plan for that and adjust. If he comes in the middle of the first quarter and leaves in the fourth quarter or if he decides use the restroom, whatever it is, you have to be prepared for that."

Sarkisian went on to reveal that the Miami Hurricanes and the Indiana Hoosiers actually had to deal with these issues during the national championship game.

Needless to say, Sarkisian's revelation seemingly caught the sports world off guard, as several high-profile sports commentators, analysts, and personalities had no idea that this was even an issue.

"Have to admit, didn't know this one…" wrote former ESPN star Gene Wojciechowski.

"I did not realize football helmet communication gets shut off if the president gets up to go to the bathroom," wrote Chris Vianni of The Athletic.

"So if the president decides to go pee during an important 3rd down or a late offensive possession the comms go out and they have to signal in the plays? Seems like a big deal," wrote Geoff Schwartz of Fox Sports.

"I get why that's in place, but it's CRAZY for teams to deal with that. Wonder how the Lions/Commanders navigated that last year," wrote Detroit Lions beat writer Jeremy Reisman of Pride of Detroit.

"That's actually kind of wild," wrote NFL insider Albert Breer.

"It's gotta be like using your phone on the NYC subway with this president's bladder," joked broadcaster and journalist Master Tesfatsion of Bleacher Report and Amazon Prime Video.

It's certainly a unique challenge. We'll have to see whether or not it comes into play on Saturday.

title: Texas A&M vs. LSU Preview: Tigers and Aggies Meet in a Massive SEC Showdown

fullText:
No. 10 LSU and No. 23 Texas A&M enter Saturday night looking to respond after suffering their first losses of the season.

Both teams are 2-1 overall and 0-1 in SEC play. LSU fell 32-24 at Ole Miss after rallying from a 24-7 deficit, while Texas A&M was upset 31-21 at home by Kentucky. With both teams already carrying an SEC loss, Saturday's matchup has added importance early in the conference race.

This will be Lane Kiffin's fourth consecutive night game at Tiger Stadium and his first home game since LSU's emotional trip to Ole Miss.

The Tigers have been productive offensively, averaging more than 500 total yards per game through three games. Quarterback Sam Leavitt has also shown the ability to make plays through the air and with his legs.

However, LSU will be without two important contributors. Defensive back Dashawn Spears suffered a season-ending knee injury against Ole Miss, while tight end Trey'Dez Green is expected to miss multiple games after suffering a knee injury. Green had 14 catches for 222 yards and a touchdown through three games.

The Aggies are coming off a disappointing loss to Kentucky in which they were outscored 21-0 in the third quarter.

Quarterback Marcel Reed struggled in the defeat, throwing two interceptions and completing 33 of 54 passes for 265 yards. Despite the performance, head coach Mike Elko has continued to express confidence in his quarterback, pointing to Reed's 15-6 record as a starter.

Texas A&M will also be without wide receiver Terry Bussey, who suffered a lower-body injury against Kentucky and is out for the remainder of the season. Bussey entered the game with seven catches for 92 yards and also contributed on special teams.

Texas A&M won last year's meeting 49-25 in Baton Rouge, making this LSU's opportunity to respond on its home field.

The Aggies have also won the last two meetings between the programs, while the teams are tied at five wins apiece over their last 10 matchups.

That history adds another layer to an already important SEC matchup.

The game kicks off at 7:30 p.m. ET Saturday at Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge and will air on ABC.

With both teams coming off losses, Saturday night gives LSU and Texas A&M an immediate opportunity to get back on track in the SEC. The atmosphere in Baton Rouge should be intense, and the matchup between LSU's defense and Texas A&M's offense could go a long way toward determining how the game unfolds.

title: Disgraced Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes approved for halfway house move in 2027
description:
Theranos founder and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has been approved for placement in a community correction center, or halfway house, and is scheduled to be placed there next year, according to an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System, ABC News has learned.
Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027, according to the notification.
Benjamin Fanjoy/Bloomberg via Getty Images - PHOTO: Elizabeth Holmes, founder of Theranos Inc., arrives at federal court in San Jose, Calif.
fullText:
Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center.

Theranos founder and convicted felon Elizabeth Holmes has been approved for placement in a community correction center, or halfway house, and is scheduled to be placed there next year, according to an update from the Department of Justice's Victim Notification System, ABC News has learned.

Holmes is scheduled to be placed in the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027, according to the notification.

When reached for comment on Wednesday, the Federal Bureau of Prisons said in a statement that it "does not discuss the conditions of confinement for any individual, including release plans."

"Additionally, per BOP policy, specific designation information cannot be released until after an individual arrives at their designated institution," the statement continued.

BOP said several factors go into assigning individuals to facilities, including "the level of security and supervision required, medical or programmatic needs, separation or security considerations necessary for the individual’s safety, and other relevant factors, such as proximity to the individual’s release residence."

Holmes was originally sentenced in 2022 to 11 years and 3 months in prison for defrauding investors with false claims about her company's blood-testing technology.

Her sentence has since been reduced to 10 years and 3 months, and she is now scheduled to be released on Feb. 22, 2030. According to the Victim Notification System, upon her release, Holmes will reside in Austin, Texas, and be supervised by the United States Probation Office there.

The new release date was the result of a retroactive change to federal sentencing guidelines and earned time through the First Step Act.

"To be clear, this sentence reduction does not diminish the enormity of Holmes's crimes, nor does it ignore the significant negative impact her conduct has had on the community," U.S. District Judge Edward Davila wrote in a March order granting a motion to reduce her sentence. "The hundreds of millions of dollars in losses caused by Holmes's fraud speak for themselves. And though unquantifiable, the echoes of the immense reputational damage that the innovative industry in Silicon Valley suffered as a consequence of Holmes's deception still reverberate to this day. Holmes's revised sentence continues to reflect a just punishment for her serious offense and serves as a reminder that the scales of justice will balance."

Holmes was found guilty of three counts of wire fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud while at the helm of Theranos. She reported to prison in May 2023.

Last year, a U.S. appeals court upheld the fraud convictions and $452 million restitution order for Holmes and her second-in-command, Ramesh "Sunny" Balwani.

The two had argued the court committed several legal errors and violated their constitutional rights during their separate trials. The three-judge panel for the appeals court rejected their claims, finding that any errors were harmless or that their arguments failed to show any violation.

Holmes is the subject of a forthcoming documentary by filmmaker Nathan Fielder, "You Can See Everything." In a new trailer for the film released Wednesday, Holmes maintained that she "did not" do anything wrong.

She participated in the documentary in 2023, before reporting to prison.

fullText:
(Corrects Trump's approval rating in paragraph three)

DONNA, Texas, Sept 23 (Reuters) - South Texas unfurls in long stretches of highways across flat landscapes dotted with pump jacks, mesquite trees, and gas stations sporting prices that voters swear should not be this high. This territory swung heavily to Donald Trump in 2024 — but may shift again in 2026.

From the outskirts of San Antonio, through historic, sprawling ranchlands to the border city of McAllen, Reuters traveled more than 360 miles (580 km) and ‌spoke to more than 30 Latino voters, who shared a similar refrain: as President, Trump had a chance to lower prices across this expanse, where trucks and beef barbacoa are king, and failed.

Many are no longer convinced the Republican Party is looking out for people like ‌them. Frustration over economic pressures and Trump's immigration agenda is rising, exposing cracks in what Republican officials hoped was a durable political realignment among Latino Americans. Trump's approval rating nationwide has fallen to 32%, the lowest since returning to office, according to the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll.

That uncertainty poses a problem for Texas Republicans, who redrew congressional maps last year betting the Latino ​contingent who helped power Trump's 2024 win would remain in their column.

Now, they're grappling with whether this notoriously swingy voting group may snap back to Democrats in the Lone Star State as they have in other parts of the country in off-year and special elections, said David Wasserman, elections analyst at the nonpartisan forecaster Cook Political Report.

Texas Republicans sought to make several districts more favorable to their candidates ahead of the 2026 elections, basing their changes on Trump's 2024 performance, the strongest showing among Latino voters by a Republican presidential candidate this century. Rather than dilute Latino voting power, many of the newly configured districts remained heavily Latino, including Texas' 15th and 35th Congressional Districts.

In District 15, Latinos account for 74.5% of the citizen voting-age population. In District 35, they make up 51.6%, according to the state's redistricting analysis. Yet both districts have become more competitive, with political prognostication site Sabato's Crystal Ball rating the 15th District a Toss-up and the 35th District Lean Republican. ‌Cook Political rates the 15th Lean Republican.

An August 2026 Texas Southern University poll found Democratic congressional candidates leading ⁠in three South Texas districts, including the 15th. Interviews with almost 50 analysts, activists, pollsters and voters back up the idea that some Latinos in South Texas who voted for Trump appear open to Democrats.

One of those is Saúl Guajardo, 53, of McAllen, who voted for Trump three times.

"I used to be a conservative, far-right," he said. "I'm more open than ever before to vote Democrat."

Guajardo said he and his wife Terrie live paycheck-to-paycheck, despite steady incomes. Gasoline is a big ⁠weight, as the average price of a gallon was $4.09 in the McAllen area as of September 22, according to AAA data.

Terrie said Trump's strict immigration enforcement "crackdown" was too harsh for people who simply want to work in the United States, as his policies have permanently separated some families trying to make a life in the U.S.

Polling suggests many Latinos are souring on Republicans. A September poll of 1,000 Latinos in Texas conducted for Cook Political and TelevisaUnivision found that 18% of Latinos who voted for Trump no longer support him, and almost two-thirds of Latino voters would be less likely to vote for candidates who support Trump's immigration policies.

For both parties, those shifts explain both ​the ​promise and peril of Latino voters. Their support has often proved less dependent on party loyalty than on whether they believe elected officials will improve their economic circumstances.

"It's not ​one of these that you're talking to a wall because they're all going to vote Democrat or they're all ‌going to vote Republican," said Daniel Alegre, CEO of Spanish-language media company TelevisaUnivision. "They're all going to vote for the person who is going to make their lives better."

Republicans reject the premise that Latino voters are moving away from them. Christian Martinez, the National Republican Congressional Committee's national Hispanic press secretary, said Democrats spent years responding to declining support among Hispanic voters with "denial, excuses, and condescension," instead of addressing concerns that drove many working-class voters toward Republicans.

The risk that redistricting backfires is particularly clear in the 15th District, which in its reconfigured form would have given Trump an 18-point win in 2024, compared with a two-point margin in 2020 and a 14-point loss in his first election in 2016.

That district's incumbent, Republican Monica De La Cruz, is facing a unique opponent in Democratic singer Bobby Pulido, whose celebrity status predates his entry into politics. His signature hit, "Desvelado," has nearly 610 million Spotify streams, and he has won two Latin Grammy Awards.

His economic message and crossover appeal have turned the district into one of the state's most closely watched races. A late August Texas Southern University poll had Pulido leading De La Cruz by five percentage points.

Dressed in a cowboy hat, blue jeans and cowboy boots, Pulido crisscrosses South Texas ‌on weekends, hopping from one quinceañera, a traditional 15th birthday celebration for girls in Latino communities, to another. His surprise — and free — appearances often end with a gift for ​the celebrant: a white hat with pink lettering reading "Make Quinceañeras Great Again."

Pulido said Democrats lost ground with Latino voters in South Texas because they failed to address the economic concerns ​that matter most to working families, though he said both major parties often misread the electorate.

"As a Democrat, I think that we misunderstand ​the Hispanic vote and I think, honestly, I think Republicans don't get it either," Pulido told Reuters. "We don't want handouts, we're very proud. We just want an opportunity to go work and make something and provide for our families, and then ‌work towards our kids prospering better than we did."

On August 1, Pulido surprised Melody Silva and roughly 200 ​relatives and friends gathered for her quinceañera. They screamed when he appeared at the ​top of a staircase and cheered louder when he mentioned his congressional race.

"He's got such great roots here in the Valley," said Michael Silva, Melody's father and a police officer in McAllen. "I feel like he's not just representing the Valley, but representing the raza, you know, the people, for us — locals."

His name recognition appears to be one of his greatest strengths. Among the dozen voters Reuters spoke to at a monthly outdoor market roughly 180 miles (290 km) north in rural Beeville, Pulido's name was as ubiquitous as the summer heat.

De La Cruz's campaign ​did not respond to requests for comment.

Ramon Barrera, 36, known as "The Texas Tea Guy" on social media, sees ‌the shift in sentiment. He posts short TikTok updates "spilling the tea" about politics and community issues, crisscrossing South Texas in his Dodge Ram 3500 to talk to locals, along with hunting for old furniture to refurbish.

He voted for Trump for the first time ​in 2024, describing himself as conservative but not strongly aligned with either party. He said Trump's term has been a disappointment, opening the door for him to vote for Pulido and Gina Hinojosa, the Democrat running for governor against Republican Greg Abbott, who is ​seeking a fourth consecutive term.

"The S&P 500 looks great, but our wallets don't," he said.

title: Rick Barnes is all Vol this weekend with Texas coming to town
description: Another Tennessee-Texas moment for Rick Barnes
fullText:
Tennessee-Texas is far from a traditional rivalry, but it's certainly interesting on a couple of different levels. You have the never ending 'who is the real UT' question, which will never be agreed upon by the two fanbases. That dilemma is funny too, considering the schools have only ever met three times playing football, each coming more than a half century ago in Cotton Bowls.

And then there's Rick Barnes — the legendary coach that Texas grew stale with after 17 years leading the men's basketball program. Barnes made the NCAA Tournament 16 times during his time in Austin, reaching the Final Four back in 2003. However, Barnes didn't make it past the first weekend during his final seven seasons. Texas pulled the trigger on change, and Tennessee was there to happily give Barnes a new home when they desperately needed stability.

Barnes may have even found a better fit in Knoxville, making three straight Elite Eight appearances over the last three seasons. With his old school coming to town this weekend, Barnes was clear who he'll be cheering on.

"Well, I'm pulling for the Tennessee Volunteers," Rick Barnes said on Tuesday. "I can tell you that. And what I would tell you, someone asked me the other day about it. You know, I spent 17 years in Texas, had wonderful friends there. A bunch of them will come in. I doubt I will see them all.

"Really good friends with (Texas AD) Chris Del Conte. I love the guy. He and I got to be buddies when I was in Texas and he was at TCU. And he has done just an incredible job in Texas. And what Danny White has done here, I look at those two guys as being guys that I think if people would listen to them, we could get some things done because they both see things in a different way."

No surprise Barnes is pulling for the Volunteers on Saturday. He's embraced everything about Tennessee from the jump, building the basketball program back from the ground up. He's survived some bad athletic administrations through the years, and now is reaping the benefits of the department finally being on solid ground.

"Obviously, I like to see us because I love Josh Heupel and the way he's building here," Barnes continued. "I think Texas is No. 1. That's why we play the games, right? But, again, I just have so many fond memories of my time in Texas.

"The last 11 years here have been 11 of the best years of my life. And the people I've met wouldn't trade it for anything."

fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas — The ICE officer who shot a Venezuelan man in Austin on Sunday, leaving a bullet lodged in his back, was issued a body camera but was not wearing it during the shooting, two officials with the Department of Homeland Security told NBC News.

The officials said it was not clear why the officer was not wearing his body camera. Another ICE officer who was in the same vehicle was wearing a body camera, the officials said. That camera captured partial footage of the incident, but the footage does not include the moment of the shooting, the officials said.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, was shot early Sunday afternoon by an ICE officer while making deliveries as a DoorDash driver. He was taken to a hospital and, four hours after he was shot, was taken into immigration custody at the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, his attorney said. The bullet remains in his back.

On Tuesday, a federal judge granted an emergency order temporarily blocking deportation proceedings against Garcés Pérez, according to his attorney, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch.

The Travis County District Attorney’s Office also sent a letter to DHS and ICE leadership requesting that Garcés Pérez be allowed to remain in the country since he is “a material witness” in their criminal investigation into the shooting.

Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis shared on Tuesday evening some of the first video footage obtained by the department as part on their probe into the shooting. The videos came from an off-duty officer who captured part of the encounter between ICE and Garcés Pérez, as well as the sound of three gunshots, using his personal dash cam and cellphone.

After this, the off-duty officer alerted his colleagues to the shooting, allowing Austin police to quickly respond to the scene.

Davis said they are seeking the public’s help in obtaining any video evidence that can help them piece together the pursuit that preceded the shooting.

The day after he was shot, Garcés Pérez began “experiencing an inability to move his arm,” attorney Lincoln-Goldfinch said on social media. He was taken to the hospital Monday afternoon for several hours and then sent back to the detention center, she said.

The DHS did not respond to requests for comment about Lincoln-Goldfinch’s statements.

Earlier Monday, Garcés Pérez told a news conference via phone from detention that he was in a lot of pain and wasn’t getting the medical care he needed.

Lincoln-Goldfinch alleged in a social media post that after Garcés Pérez spoke out at the news conference, guards at the detention center “forcibly took the tablet from his hands, revoked his communication privileges, and moved him out of the infirmary into an isolated room with a flat bed that cannot be adjusted like a medical bed.”

He was then taken to the hospital around 5 p.m. after losing his ability to move his arm, she said.

“Wilber reports that he was handcuffed, shackled at the ankles, placed in a waist chain, and handled roughly during that transfer,” she said in the post.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said Garcés Pérez told her on Tuesday morning that doctors spoke to him about his care and gave him morphine for his pain.

“We now understand that the gunshot fractured his clavicle and that he has significant swelling and is wearing a sling,” she wrote. “We still do not have clarity about the cause or extent of the loss of movement he experienced.”

The attorney said Garcés Pérez was discharged from the hospital around midnight and taken back to the detention center, where he is receiving Tylenol and ibuprofen for his ongoing pain.

“He remains in isolation, on a flat bed, and without the tablet he previously used to communicate,” she said.

“We are asking for his communication privileges to be immediately restored and for him to be provided an appropriate medical bed and adequate medical care,” she said. “Most importantly, we are continuing to advocate for Wilber’s IMMEDIATE release.”

Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, said on social media that “despite losing movement on his left side and having a bullet lodged next to his spine, ICE has forced Wilber Rafael out of the hospital and back to the South Texas ICE Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas.”

He said that he and Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, would visit Garcés Pérez on Wednesday, check on his condition and demand his release.

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement late Sunday that Garcés Pérez was in stable condition and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S.

A senior administration official told NBC News on Monday that Garcés Pérez did not have a criminal history beyond being in the country illegally.

According to Lincoln-Goldfinch, Garcés Pérez entered the country legally and was seeking asylum. She said Garcés Pérez had filed a change of address in immigration court, but received a notice to appear in court at the old address and never got it. Because he missed his immigration hearing, Garcés Pérez was ordered deported in absentia, according to his attorney.

On Monday, Lincoln-Goldfinch shared Garcés Pérez’s account of the shooting, saying he was making a delivery when “an unmarked black truck sideswiped him.” She said he didn’t know it was ICE as the truck chased him as he tried to make a U-turn, and then “pulled him out of the car.”

Previously, DHS has accused immigrants involved in shootings with ICE of using their cars as weapons while fleeing agents, without offering evidence of its claims. But it did not make the accusation in the case of Garcés Pérez or in the case of Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was fatally shot in Biddeford, Maine, in July during a traffic stop.

ICE Director David Venturella previously told NBC News that every ICE officer and agent would be equipped with body cameras by the end of August, adding the agency would allow the “expedited release” of bodycam footage “when appropriate.” Further delaying that timeline is the possibility of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin potentially switching or adding new vendors for body cameras.

A person who witnessed the aftermath of the shooting but who requested anonymity because he is going through immigration proceedings told Noticias Telemundo that he was waiting on customers at the ice cream shop where he works when he heard gunshots and ran outside, where he saw immigration agents surrounding a car.

“I approached the car and saw a man who looked sad and with his eyes full of tears. I asked him what happened to him, and he just told me, ‘I was shot in the back,’” said the person, a Mexican immigrant who has lived in the U.S. for more than two decades.

“You aren’t prepared to see someone like that. It makes you very angry, it pains you and you don’t know what to do,” he said.

A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing each other. The sedan appears to be damaged on the passenger side.

At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection.

Another video shows the blue sedan with its driver’s side door open and Garcés Pérez hunched over in the driver’s seat, holding his left upper chest, near his shoulder, as multiple law enforcement officers gather around.

The woman taking the video says, “Why did he do that to him?” The officers tell her that an ambulance is coming.

The video shows Garcés Pérez being taken out of the car and handcuffed behind his back. The agents make him sit on the ground. There appears to be a large bloodstain down his back. The officers cut open the back of his shirt, revealing a bullet hole.

An officer asks the woman taking the video if she saw what happened. In Spanish, she replies that “they just shot him because he didn’t want to stop” his vehicle.

“This is unjust,” she says as she’s recording the video.

Julia Ainsley reported from Washington, D.C., Daniella Silva from New York and Albinson Linares from Austin, Texas.

An ICE officer shot Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old native of Venezuela who federal officials said has a deportation order, in the upper torso on Sunday afternoon while Garces Perez was working for DoorDash, according to local authorities and his attorney.
The shooting was the latest involving federal agents enforcing President Trump's crackdown on illegal immigration and has sparked protests in Texas, as well as calls for accountability and a transparent, independent investigation.

title: Man shot by ICE being detained with bullet still in his back, lawyer says
description:
A Venezuelan man who was shot by an immigration officer while delivering a DoorDash order in Austin, Texas, was transferred from the hospital to a detention center with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer said Monday.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was shot in the back by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer after the officer sideswiped the 28-year-old's car early Sunday afternoon, attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told reporters at a Monday news conference. Garces Perez was then taken to the hospital, and his family was notified four hours later that he had been taken to the South Texas Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, approximately a two-hour drive away from Austin, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. 
Garces Perez spoke by phone during the news conference, saying in Spanish that he was in a lot of pain. He explained that the bullet wasn't removed because it was lodged close to his spine.

title: Elon Musk's spending draws additional attention to Texas Senate race
description:

fullText:
The last time Elon Musk sank money into an election, he played a starring role in the 2025 state Supreme Court race in Wisconsin. He donned an oversized cheese hat, offered $1 million checks to voters, and he and affiliated groups poured at least $20 million into the contest.

In the end, the conservative candidate lost by 10 points in what was widely viewed as a rebuke of Musk and the Trump administration.

Now, the richest person in the world is back boosting Republican candidates in critical midterm elections, including a bruising Senate race in Texas where Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton is facing Democrat James Talarico, who had initially far outraised him and remains close in polling.

But that financial tide is quickly turning — with Musk’s help.

Unlike in Wisconsin, Musk has so far stayed out of the spotlight in Texas, even though he lives in the state, has based his companies Tesla and SpaceX there, and employs about 20,000 people. He hasn’t announced plans for any in-person events, or teased — as he did in Wisconsin — that he’d be handing out $1 million checks to voters.

Privately, Republicans say they want Musk to keep his distance. In interviews, more than half a dozen Republican strategists involved in the Texas Senate race say they hope Musk follows his 2024 model of electoral involvement, which led to a Republican sweep of the White House and Congress. Then, Musk spent more than $250 million on Donald Trump and his party.

Republicans believe Democrats will attempt to turn Musk into a boogeyman if he takes on a higher-profile role in Texas or other battlegrounds. One Republican consultant involved in the Texas Senate race said that was the perception in Wisconsin.

“He came in super late, and it was very public,” said the consultant, who, like others interviewed for this article, were granted anonymity to speak candidly. “Elon spending money became the story, which I think maybe was a mistake.”

A different Republican strategist involved in Texas campaigns said those around Musk learned from the experience.

“Did Elon bring some things to the Wisconsin race that hampered things? Probably,” the person added. “But I think they will adjust for that.”

Democrats, however, say they welcome Musk more publicly entering the fray in Texas.

“Elon, bring it. You’ve failed in Wisconsin. You’ll fail in Texas,” said Nathan Johnson, a Democrat running to replace Paxton as attorney general. “I’m not afraid of Elon bringing his political money here. All these policies favor him or people like him.”

An in-your-face Musk campaign would play into Talarico’s narrative that the real American divide isn’t left versus right but “top versus bottom,” with elites and billionaires exerting control over the working class, they say.

“James is running largely on costs and corruption,” Luke Warford, a Texas-based Democratic strategist and chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, said of Talarico. “The idea of the richest man in the world coming in late to try to buy the election and save Ken Paxton really plays into James Talarico’s argument.”

The Texas Senate race has all the makings of a contest that would attract Musk. The conservative narrative building against Talarico amplifies his past remarks in support of transgender people, including his comment that “God is nonbinary.” Talarico told Fox News he was being “provocative” and was trying to convey that one cannot use “human categories to define God.”

Musk has spoken publicly about his own transgender daughter, Vivian Jenna Wilson, saying she was “not a girl” and was figuratively “dead.” He also alleged that he had been “tricked” into authorizing trans-related medical treatment for her when she was 16. Wilson previously told NBC News that Musk was an absent father who was cruel to her as a child for being queer and feminine.

At this point, Musk’s America PAC has not said how much it will invest in Texas, but a person with knowledge of the group’s thinking indicated that as of now, the Paxton-Talarico contest was not slotted to receive more focus than other Senate or congressional races the group is investing in across the country, saying “every state and district where we are spending is a priority.”

To date, America PAC has spent nearly $5.2 million on digital ads, mail, live calls and pamphleting in Texas, but that number is expected to significantly climb.

In all, the super PAC has spent $14.7 million on congressional races, including seven Senate races and nearly three dozen House races. The group has spent the most money on the Texas Senate race, followed by nearly $3 million on Senate races in Ohio and Michigan.

National Republican groups long knew they would have to provide air cover for Paxton because of an initial fundraising disadvantage to Talarico, who had $21 million in cash on hand compared to Paxton’s $1.7 million at the end of June, according to campaign finance reports. Today, a flood of Republican money is pouring in from several sources and the balance has suddenly tipped in Paxton’s favor.

“America PAC is working in full coordination with the entire GOP apparatus and is investing in the states and districts that will decide control of the House and Senate,” America PAC spokesman Andrew Romeo said in a statement. “Our only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington and stopping the lunatic left from bringing us back to the days of open borders, rampant crime, and woke policies.”

Paxton’s status as a scandal-plagued candidate who has been impeached and indicted — coupled with the fact he’s coming off a contentious primary against Sen. John Cornyn and much of the Republican Party establishment, aside from Trump — makes him among the most vulnerable front-line Senate Republican candidates in a state where Democrats have not won a statewide post in three decades.

After Trump’s late endorsement helped propel Paxton over Cornyn, groups like the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, and the National Republican Senatorial Committee, were left scrambling. The election cycle budgets were, in part, built on the idea that Cornyn would not need nearly as much national fundraising help.

“Cornyn had his own fundraising machine, he could raise a lot of money on his own, so it was going to make things easier to cover other important close races,” said a Republican consultant familiar with the thought process. “I know they [Elon] are focused more on the ground game stuff. MAGA Inc. is on digital and mail. This pretty much turned out the way we thought it would. It’s an expensive endeavor and a team and multigroup effort.”

The pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC has pumped at least $15 million into TV ads that have included hitting Talarico on previous votes involving China.

So far, MAGA Inc. has spent $10 million in the state to help boost Paxton, its second-biggest single-state investment.

The group did not return a request for comment, but in an interview with NBC News last week, MAGA Inc. chief James Blair said the group had booked $10 million worth of TV ad time in Texas. Blair noted the previous disparity in spending, with Talarico and related groups pummeling Paxton on TV.

“The fact is Ken Paxton had $100 million spent against him in the primary,” Blair said. “Talarico had $0 spent against him in the primary, and that has an impact on candidate images that takes time to rectify. But the resources … have begun to be deployed now in earnest [and] will take care of that problem.”

A veteran GOP official directly involved in the race contended that the shift toward spending in Texas did not take away from other battlegrounds.

“This spending will not take away from other investments,” the official said. “This came from a collection of Texas folks very committed to making sure that seat remains Republican. They see the polling, and that James Talarico is so extreme. No one wants to see Texas turn blue.”

When asked about the onslaught of money headed toward Talarico, spokesman JT Ennis said, “Billionaire-backed dark money groups are lying about James because they’re scared of the people-powered movement we’re building to fix this broken, corrupt political system.”

fullText:
An ICE officer shot and seriously wounded a Venezuelan man Sunday afternoon as he was delivering food in Austin, Texas, his lawyer said.

The man was taken to a local hospital and was “in serious but stable condition” after being shot in the torso, Austin-Travis County EMS Chief Robert Luckritz said at a news conference earlier.

The White House referred NBC News to the Department of Homeland Security for comment. A spokesperson for the DHS, the federal agency to which Immigration and Customs Enforcement belongs, said in a statement late Sunday that the man was stable and was in federal custody pending removal from the U.S.

Immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch identified him as Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28, and said he was an asylum seeker who entered the country through a parole program.

“Today at 12:30, Wilber called his wife to tell her that he had been shot,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said in an interview. “And he was yelling in agony, and the call cut off. That was all she knew.”

The DHS spokesperson said Garcés Perez entered the country illegally under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal, adding that Homeland Security Investigations, with help from the FBI, will lead an investigation into the shooting.

The shooting occurred around 1 p.m. in North Austin.

Texas Department of Public Safety spokesperson Sheridan Nolen said the agency received a request for assistance from ICE for a vehicle pursuit involving a blue Toyota Corolla.

A social media video verified by NBC News captures the sound of tires screeching followed by a person exiting a dark-colored SUV as a blue sedan is stopped next to it, both vehicles facing one another.

At least three gunshots are heard as the person approaches the sedan and runs up to it as it slowly lurches forward. The video shows the person standing next to the sedan’s driver’s side as it stops in front of an intersection. The sedan also appears to be damaged on the passenger side.

The shooting occurred before DPS troopers arrived at the scene, Nolen said.

“Once they arrived, DPS Troopers immediately began assisting partner law enforcement agencies in performing medical treatment on the driver of the Toyota Corolla,” she said in a statement.

Lincoln-Goldfinch, who is representing Garcés Perez, said lawyers for the hospital where he was treated indicated he had been released, though she wasn’t sure at the time to whom.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said she was with his wife at the hospital earlier, hoping to get information on his condition, but they were escorted from the premises.

“We not only were lied to and told that he wasn’t there, but we were thrown off the hospital grounds by several officers who treated us as trespassers,” she said.

Austin Mayor Kirk Watson showed up several hours later and had a hospital administrator call Lincoln-Goldfinch and the man’s wife, the lawyer said. The administrator confirmed he had been released to ICE, she said.

The hospital, Dell Seton Medical Center at The University of Texas, did not respond to a request for comment.

“We are deeply concerned that his wife and family have not been permitted to see him and have not received a meaningful update regarding his current condition or whereabouts,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a statement earlier.

Garcés Perez, who Lincoln-Goldfinch said lives in Austin, is a DoorDash driver. In an email, a company spokesperson confirmed Garcés Perez was making a delivery at the time, adding that DoorDash is investigating and would not release more information “at this time.”

Lincoln-Goldfinch said her priority, and that of Garcés Perez’s family, is to find him and verify his condition.

“No one has told me or Wilber’s wife what the treatment was or how he’s doing,” she said, “and I feel very confident he is in a lot of pain right now as we speak.”

DHS has not provided any information about whether the ICE agent involved was wearing a body camera or if the man was the target of an operation or has any criminal background other than an immigration violation.

Lincoln-Goldfinch said his wife, who has legal status, indicated her husband has no criminal history.

The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.

Watson, Austin’s mayor, said the city’s police department was not involved in the incident.

Police Chief Lisa Davis said a “small foot pursuit” had occurred and that Austin police investigators were on the scene. Davis added that she was in contact with Homeland Security Investigations and other state law enforcement agencies.

“A person being shot on the streets of Austin by someone purporting to be law enforcement, particularly when it’s ICE, is something that causes me to be unhappy and angry,” Watson said at the news conference. “While I’m unhappy and I’m angry about it, I’m not surprised at all.”

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, demanded an independent investigation, the release of any body camera footage and “accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law.”

“Over and over, ICE has shot people and then lied about what happened. We can see the lies with our own eyes. We will demand truth, transparency and accountability,” he said in a post on X.

In a letter addressed to DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Acting ICE Director David Venturella, Casar insisted on receiving a Congressional briefing by Sept. 28.

James Talarico, who is running as the Democratic candidate for one of Texas’ U.S. Senate seats, said he is “closely following” reports of the shooting, and requested an investigation and all available footage.

U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, demanded “full accountability.”

“Trump has allowed ICE to flood our streets and put our communities in harms way again and again,” he said in a post on X.

In reaction to the shooting, the League of United Latin American Citizens — the largest Latino civil rights organization in the U.S. — called on Congress to establish an independent oversight of immigration enforcement.

Watson said he has asked for the city of Austin to be involved in any forthcoming investigations so that the police department can “be in a position to offer clear third-party eyes and expertise”

In a statement, the Travis County District Attorney’s Office requested to be “co-equal partners in the investigation” and to receive cooperation from the federal government.

Protesters who gathered at the site of the shooting on Sunday afternoon and evening, next to an elevated stretch of Highway 183, shouted anti-ICE slogans in English and Spanish. Some carried signs that said, “Stop ICE murder,” “Moms against ICE” and “Abolish ICE.”

One woman, who said she has lived in Austin for 33 years, told NBC News earlier Sunday that she has never witnessed an incident like this and it “broke my heart.”

The protest was punctuated with the sounds of drums, and someone could be heard saying, “They don’t want you to be here,” via loudspeaker.

Late Sunday night, the gathering roiled with tension, and Texas Department of Public Safety troopers responded by deploying tear gas and, in some instances, tackling protesters.

Protesters had dispersed and troopers appeared to have exited the area by 11 p.m. local time.

The shooting comes two months after an ICE officer fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national, in Houston during an attempted traffic stop to conduct an immigration arrest. DHS has said Salgado Araujo was in the country illegally and attempted to run over agents, but it has not provided evidence of its claims.

title: ICE agent shoots and wounds man in Austin, authorities say
description:
— A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.
The man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the capital city's north side, Austin officials said at a news conference. 
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn’t respond to repeated requests for details.
fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.

The man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the capital city's north side, Austin officials said at a news conference.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn't respond to repeated requests for details.

City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said while briefing reporters along with the city's mayor and other officials.

Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department to have a role in the investigation so it can provide "clear, third-party eyes" in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own.

Austin residents have "a right to feel safe in their city," Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.

The chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident but added that her department's special investigation unit was at the scene.

The Texas Department of Public Safety said it received a request from ICE for assistance in a vehicle pursuit around 12:50 p.m. By the time DPS troopers arrived, the shooting had already taken place, the department said in a statement Sunday evening.

An immigration attorney representing the man's family identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man.

Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video posted to her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and no final order of removal from the U.S., but she later told The Associated Press that she did not know his current immigration status.

The man's family has struggled to get any information from the hospital about his status or location, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Just before 7 p.m., the man's wife was informed by the hospital's attorney that the man had been released into ICE custody a few hours earlier, Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote in a text to AP.

"No one bothered to update her," she wrote.

It wasn't immediately clear if the man remained hospitalized while in ICE custody or if he had been transferred elsewhere.

A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes. The car was towed away in the early evening and traffic began moving again.

A large law enforcement presence was present along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying, "Nobody is safe" and, on the other side, "ICE Nazi."

Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: "We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that's involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state."

The office of Travis County District Attorney José Pompa Garza asked that local police and prosecutors be included in the investigation.

"We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence," the DA's office said in a statement Sunday evening.

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar told reporters. "For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here."

The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.

Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine. The officer is an Army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and never should have been given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relatives told AP.

The administration's enforcement efforts were widely condemned last winter after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

Weber reported from Los Angeles and Boone from Boise, Idaho. Contributing were Associated Press journalists Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, Rhode Island and Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis.

title: Texas stays No. 1, A&M plunges and UH stays ranked in latest AP Top 25 poll

title: Gas prices are squeezing voters as Trump calls the increase a small price to pay

fullText:
EDINBURG, Texas (AP) — Quinten Martinez, pumping gas under a hot South Texas sun, remembers a time when fueling up didn't require difficult decisions.

"Is it going to be groceries this week?" asked the 28-year-old Amazon delivery driver as he watched the numbers tick higher. "Is it gonna be getting gas in our tank to go to work?"

He shook his head when asked about President Donald Trump's assertion last week that higher gas prices are a small price to pay for the war with Iran.

"I don't feel like it's a good trade-off," Martinez said. "I don't feel like this is good for anyone."

Voters across the country, and across the political spectrum, tend to agree.

Interviews with voters in several states, along with a fresh round of national polling, reveal an overwhelming sense of frustration that skyrocketing gas prices — a direct result of Trump's war — are creating serious and sustained financial hardships for America's working class.

The acute concerns are adding to a bad political environment that may be worsening for Trump and his Republican Party as early voting gets underway in the November midterm elections.

Historically, the party holding the White House has suffered major losses in midterms. Today, seven weeks before Election Day, Republican candidates at all levels are struggling with the additional burden of Trump's weak approval ratings, an unpopular foreign conflict and an affordability crisis that Trump and his congressional allies had promised to fix.

But when Trump campaigned in North Carolina on Wednesday, he played down the impact of surging gas prices.

"You have a little higher. It's a very inexpensive price to pay for what we've done," Trump said of the war, which he describes as critical to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. "Remember that. It's a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more."

Despite what Trump says, there are few things that may matter more this election year than the price of a gallon of gasoline, according to political operatives in both parties.

Gas prices are moving sharply in the wrong direction at a time of year when drivers typically get some relief. The national average for a gallon of gas reached $4.48 on Friday, according to AAA, up roughly 17 cents over the last week, 40 cents in a month and $1.27 from a year ago.

"Gas prices matter because they're one of the few economic indicators voters experience and see in real time," said veteran Republican strategist Chris Wilson. "The price is literally staring them in the face several times a week. So I wouldn't minimize the frustration we're seeing, particularly among working- and middle-class voters."

Interviews with voters this week found bipartisan frustration and disappointment.

Democrats and independents were especially motivated to punish Republicans at the ballot box for their economic hardship, while some of Trump's working-class supporters pledged to support Republicans this fall, even if they weren't happy with the president's leadership on the economy.

Dan Lloyd, who voted for Trump, lamented the president's leadership as the 63-year-old carpenter paid $4.39 a gallon to fill up his pickup truck in Mesa, Arizona.

"He hurt himself stepping into this," Lloyd said of Trump. "Where's all this oil from Venezuela? I thought we were flush with gas and everything, but no. The American people eat it every time, whether it's interest rates, food, gasoline."

Still, he expects to vote Republican in the midterms.

"I think the Democratic Party has lost its way," Lloyd said. "I just feel like the whole system's on the verge of collapse."

In sweltering Edinburg, Texas, 52-year-old Kristin Jimenez shrugged off the rising price of gas after filling up her Mercedes.

"We've paid the same price under Republican presidents, we've paid this price under Democrat presidents," said Jimenez, a mother who runs a small business. She plans to vote for a Republican in because they're the "lesser of two evils."

She said gas prices aren't part of her calculation.

"We don't mind paying $8 for a cup of coffee at Starbucks, but we have a problem paying four bucks at the pump?" she said. "Make it make sense."

More than 1,500 miles to the north in central Michigan, 35-year-old Garth Johnson is trying to make ends meet running a deep-cleaning business with several gas-powered vehicles and one machine fueled by diesel, which was $6.79 a gallon as he filled up his SUV.

Johnson voted for Trump, but doesn't know what he's going to do in November. Johnson doesn't feel qualified to second-guess the president's evaluation of the war, but he's feeling financial pressure in his own life.

"I like a lot of the things he's done," Johnson said, but added "I'm a little guy and I've got to live my life."

Midterm voting was already underway on Friday in Virginia, where 60-year-old engineer Alan Johnson said Trump seems to have "no empathy" for Americans who are struggling financially.

"With the gas prices being what they are and continuing to grow, we've got to do something. Hopefully the Democrats can get into office and turn the ship around," said Johnson, who cast ballots in the morning for Democrats for the U.S. Senate and U.S. House.

In Raleigh, North Carolina, teacher Brittney Bivins sees surging gas prices as evidence that Trump and his Republican Party aren't dealing with the issues that matter most to people like her.

"He really doesn't care about everyday people," the 45-year-old said. "He can afford the gas, but most of us can't. So it feels like he's not even connected to his own people."

Bivins, who described herself as an independent, said she's eager to support Democrats this fall — especially the party's emerging democratic socialist wing.

At a gas station in Lansing, Michigan, Rina Risper spent $50 on 8 gallons of premium gas.

"When I rolled up I was in shock, actually, and said, well, maybe I should drink water instead of having that $4.99 bottle of whatever it was I was gonna get," Risper said. She thinks Trump's tariffs will make affordability even worse.

"We're not in Miami. We're in Lansing, Michigan," she said. "It's really going to impact our people."

Nationwide, more than three times as many voters say they are falling behind financially as getting ahead, according to a Fox News survey released Wednesday. By a 15 percentage point margin, Democrats are considered the party that would better handle inflation and prices at a time when the cost of living and the economy are voters' top concerns.

The Fox poll found that 61% of voters say gas prices are a major problem for their household, compared with 48% two years ago, while 52% say the same for healthcare costs, compared with 44% in 2024. Majorities also view housing costs and grocery prices as major problems, although neither has increased.

Overall, nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) say the administration has made the economy worse, compared with 52% in September 2025, including one-quarter of Republicans. Only 46% of Republicans say the administration has improved the economy, while about one-quarter don't see an impact.

Back in rural South Texas, an area where Trump's GOP made gains in recent elections, Martinez, the Amazon delivery driver, could not contain his frustration.

Trump "likes to tout that we are the best economy in the world," said Martinez, but in more rural towns, "you don't see any of the winning, you don't see any of the ups that he's talking about."

"You just see struggles for day to day life," he said.

Peoples reported from New York and Cooper from Mesa, Ariz. Associated Press writers Allen G. Breed in Raleigh, N.C., Jacqueline GaNun in Lansing, Mich., Sarah Rankin in Richmond, Va., and Nicholas Riccardi in Mason, Mich., contributed to this report.

title: 78-77 – All hands on deck as Rangers rise above Blue Jays
description: Jordan Montgomery parties like it’s fall 2023 to send Texas above .500
fullText:
The Texas Rangers scored six runs while the Toronto Blue Jays scored two runs.

At the last possible moments, the Rangers appear to have stumbled upon a winning formula.

Over the last week or so we've been privy to some victories where the Rangers have scored early, forced the opponent's hand by scratching and clawing their way on base before threatening small ball chaos, and utilized a string of heroic turns from unsuspecting pitchers who have provided multiple effective innings when forced into duty.

If that's the key to victory for Texas, they followed the plan to a Texas T tonight. The Rangers indeed scored early when Josh Jung lifted a first inning opposite field solo home run. Not satisfied with just one run, Texas plated two 

Despite having an aching ankle from getting struck by a pitch, Lopez scampered in the score the third run on a Soriano wild pitch.

Those runs felt pivotal for Texas as one out into the second inning Mr. Quality Start Cal Quantrill exited the game with an disquieting injury. I guess carrying the Rangers on his back over the last month or so has finally caught up with the recently-excellent righty. Quantrill had left his previous start with back tightness, but tonight's early exit was listed as right lat tightness, which isn't great news for the Rangers going forward.

It wasn't great news at the time either as the Rangers were suddenly without this summer's most consistent starter in a crucial game. Former playoff hero Jordan Montgomery was pressed into duty and, like many others over the last week or so, he acquitted himself well. Montgomery entered in a 1-0 game and exited after 3 2/3 innings and 51 pitches having not allowed a hit and with Texas up 3-0.

Another 2023 World Series legend followed Montgomery with Nathan Eovaldi coming in to pitch the sixth. After tossing 46 pitches on Wednesday against Boston, Eovaldi was less effective in his inning of work but he worked around a run to help bridge the bullpen to the late innings.

Like last night, the Rangers took getting scored upon personal as after Toronto made it 3-1, in the next half inning Texas scored three more runs highlighted by a Langford hurdle at home on a sac fly.

Wyatt Langford JUMPS OVER THE CATCHER AND SCORES 😮 pic.twitter.com/mMYkpcRmzg

With the majority of the game managed by a trio of historically starting pitchers, the actual relievers got to work with Robert Garcia, Chase Silseth, and Jacob Latz combining to allow one run (a seventh inning solo home run off Garcia) as the Rangers maneuvered their way to another victory on this homestand.

And so, for the first time since they were 60-59 back on Aug 10, the Rangers are back above .500. It's a fine time to do so, too, as because the Houston Astros lost tonight after allowing a seventh inning grand slam to Atlanta, the Rangers are now alone atop the American League West.

Player of the Game: Montgomery has been a bit of an unusual afterthought this season when considering his place among the October 2023 legends, but tonight he left his mark on his second stint with Texas but coming in into an emergency situation and pitching lights while the Rangers were grabbing control of the game.

For his effort, Montgomery was the winning pitcher in a big league game for the first time since Aug 2024 when he was pitching for Arizona.

title: Map shows border wall progress as new work begins
description:
New panels for the border wall are being installed in West Texas, marking the start of visible construction on a 47.3-mile project in the Big Bend region as President Donald Trump’s administration expands its barrier network along the southern border.

fullText:
New panels for the border wall are being installed in West Texas, marking the start of visible construction on a 47.3-mile project in the Big Bend region as President Donald Trump’s administration expands its barrier network along the southern border.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said the first panels for the Big Bend 1 project in Hudspeth County went up on September 15, the Associated Press first reported.

Work is beginning amid legal challenges and resistance from landowners concerned about the federal government’s plans for the remote region.

The development gives new significance to CBP’s Smart Wall map, which records 232.4 miles of various border infrastructure completed since January 20, 2025, and shows hundreds more moving through design or construction.

Newsweek contacted CBP on Saturday morning via email for further comment.

Trump directed federal agencies in January 2025 to construct temporary and permanent physical barriers supported by personnel and technology.

CBP said it is using $46.5 billion from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to develop what it calls the “Smart Wall.”

The latest work extends that program into a part of Texas where rugged terrain and private ownership have historically limited continuous fencing.

CBP’s plans can affect landowners, border communities and visitors to public spaces through new walls, roads, surveillance equipment and vehicle barriers.

Big Bend 1 is one component of CBP’s plan for approximately 175 miles of primary barrier across Hudspeth, Jeff Davis and Presidio counties.

Agency planning documents say the system may include surveillance cameras, lighting, fiber-optic and power cables, utility shelters, and access and patrol roads.

Work has moved forward first near Sierra Blanca, east of El Paso.

The other two primary wall projects shown on CBP’s map cover 62.2 miles and 56.3 miles respectively, but reporting published on September 18 said construction had not begun on those Presidio County sections.

Access to private land presents a significant complication.

Some property owners are challenging the administration’s use of eminent domain and environmental-law waivers, potentially leaving the government able to build on certain parcels but not others.

Clara Bensen of the No Big Bend Wall coalition told The Guardian that officials were moving forward even though “the plan is not fully baked,” while land disputes complicate efforts to construct a continuous barrier.

Newsweek reached out to the campaign group for further comment via email on Saturday morning.

Bob Krumenaker, a former Big Bend National Park superintendent who chairs Keep Big Bend Wild, said in The Guardian opposition had crossed party lines: “I’m very optimistic that there is a lot of support for Big Bend. This is a nonpartisan issue.”

A coalition of West Texas landowners has also filed a federal lawsuit shortly before the construction update, seeking to stop projects across the region.

CBP has published a live interactive Smart Wall map that allows people to explore individual projects and view their construction status. You can see the live map here.

CBP’s map depicts a collection of different enforcement structures, not one uninterrupted wall.

The map uses color-coded lines to distinguish bollard, vehicle and waterborne barriers from supporting infrastructure and technology-only sections without a wall.

Red marks bollard barriers, orange vehicle barriers, blue waterborne barriers, purple system attributes only; light green technology and patrol roads without a wall; and dark green technology-only coverage without a wall or road.

The categories reflect the wider mix of barriers, roads and detection technology included in CBP’s Smart Wall program.

For new primary Smart Wall, the agency lists 357.4 miles under construction, 193.1 miles awarded and 70 miles completed. Another 417.2 miles of secondary wall are being built, while 88.5 miles are awarded and 72.1 miles are finished.

Waterborne systems represent another major category, with 375.2 miles under construction, 115.4 miles awarded and 42.1 miles complete.

Replacement of existing primary barriers accounts for a smaller share.

Those figures cannot simply be combined and described as a single length of new wall.

Primary fencing, parallel secondary structures and river barriers may occupy the same general locations.

Terminology matters too. CBP uses “under construction” when wall panels or waterborne barriers are being built or deployed.

“Awarded” may mean a project remains in design, although it can also cover early construction activity.

CBP said it does not intend to install 30-foot steel bollard walls inside Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park or the Black Gap Wildlife Management Area.

Cameras, sensors and low-profile vehicle barriers are planned instead.

That distinction means construction in Hudspeth County should not be conflated with separate work proposed inside the national park.

CBP said it is coordinating with the National Park Service to maintain access to the Rio Grande and hiking trails while identifying cultural, historical and biological resources that could be affected.

The plans have drawn public protests in and around Big Bend National Park, including demonstrations at Santa Elena Canyon on August 12 and in Study Butte, Texas, on August 15, as residents and public lands advocates raised concerns about construction in the protected landscape.

Demonstrators gathered with signs opposing border infrastructure in one of West Texas’ best-known protected landscapes.

Physical barriers make up only part of the program. CBP plans approximately 538 miles of technology beside previously built barriers and about 205 miles of detection equipment near Big Bend vehicle barriers.

A further 167 miles of the border are expected to receive separately funded detection technology because terrain or remoteness makes wall construction unfavorable.

Combined with the Big Bend deployment, CBP says approximately 372 miles will be covered by technology alone.

The immediate questions are whether construction extends beyond the parcels now available to the government, how pending litigation affects the schedule and when the remaining Big Bend sections advance.

CBP cautions that mileage may change as designs and routes are finalized. Its map also does not provide project-level completion dates, final costs or independent measurements showing how each barrier type affects unlawful crossings, smuggling or migrant safety.

title: Nick Saban explains why Ohio State lost its edge at half vs. Texas

fullText:
Former Alabama football coach Nick Saban said he knew exactly why Ohio State's momentum at halftime disappeared in the second half against Texas, which led to a 20-point comeback from the Longhorns in their 24-23 win.

title: Lingering feuds threaten Democrats' bid to reclaim Congress
description:
By Nolan D. McCaskill

   With control of both chambers at stake, Democrats have sought to move past the bad blood of the primaries, but in several competitive states, influential party figures have withheld endorsements or so far declined to campaign with nominees for the November 3 US midterm elections.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, Sept 19 (Reuters) - Democrats are seeking to reclaim Congress, but lingering divisions from a bruising run-up to the November election threaten to imperil the party's attempt to claw back power from President Donald Trump's Republicans.

With control of both chambers at stake, Democrats have sought to move past the bad blood of the primaries, but in several competitive states, influential party figures have withheld endorsements or so far declined to campaign with nominees for the November 3 US midterm elections.

In ‌Maine, the governor has yet to endorse the Democratic US Senate candidate. In Texas, a congresswoman has declined to campaign alongside the state representative who defeated her in the Democratic Senate primary. In Michigan, establishment centrists are steering clear of the party's progressive Senate ‌pick. In New York, victorious democratic socialists are criticizing congressional Democrats for joining Republicans in condemning socialism. In Florida, the party has yet to rally behind its Senate nominee.

"Whether you are a progressive or an establishment Democrat or a conservative Democrat, we all have a vested interest in getting every single person over the finish line in November," said US Representative ​Summer Lee, a progressive Pennsylvania Democrat up for reelection.

If Democrats fail to unify and win at least one chamber, she warned, "all of our work after that is going to be harder."

Democrats' best path to a Senate majority requires defeating Susan Collins in Maine. Collins is widely considered the most vulnerable Republican senator in the country. But former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee, is running without the endorsement of Governor Janet Mills, a onetime Senate candidate who hoped to unseat Collins herself. Mills' office did not respond to a request for comment.

"I would say they're mostly unified," Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington, said of Maine Democrats. "The one piece of it that stands out is that Janet Mills has not endorsed Troy Jackson."

Contacted by Reuters, the Maine Democratic Party did not directly address Mills' role but cited turnout for its nominating process and energy on the ground as evidence of unity. "Maine Democrats ‌are united and focused on winning in November," said Devon Murphy-Anderson, the state party's executive director. "Troy has ⁠spent his career fighting for working Mainers and there is real energy behind his campaign to defeat Susan Collins."

In Texas, US Representative Jasmine Crockett has pledged her support to state Representative James Talarico, who defeated her in the Senate primary and is taking on Republican Ken Paxton. But Crockett has repeatedly rejected Talarico's overtures for the two to campaign together, even declining to introduce him at Texas Democrats' state convention in June.

Crockett drew criticism from ⁠social media users last week for appearing on stage in Texas with R&B singer Chris Brown, but not with Talarico, who could become the first Democrat in decades to win a statewide race in Texas. In 2009, Brown pleaded guilty to assaulting then-girlfriend Rihanna and has said domestic violence classes helped him learn from his mistakes.

Crockett has instead said she will focus on lower-profile races, arguing that will also benefit Talarico's Senate campaign.

"As the Democratic nominee, I trust that he has a plan," Crockett told CBS News this month. "I know that their plan wasn't necessarily to include his opponent."

In Michigan, lingering divisions have centered on Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, ​a ​progressive who narrowly leads Republican Mike Rogers in polling in one of the party's must-win states. Some Democrats have expressed discomfort with El-Sayed's association with controversial streamer Hasan ​Piker and with his rhetoric on Israel and Jews, and multiple prominent party figures have yet to endorse him.

After ‌their closely contested Senate primary, US Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan offered her "full support" to El-Sayed, and the two hugged at a unity breakfast the following day. An El-Sayed campaign adviser told Reuters the two camps are in regular communication and that the campaign sees Stevens "as a critical member of the coalition that will beat Mike Rogers."

But it's unclear whether Stevens will campaign with El-Sayed, and others in the party have been openly critical.

US Representative Hillary Scholten and state Senator Jeremy Moss, the Democratic nominee for a congressional seat, have not endorsed El-Sayed. Neither of their campaigns immediately responded to a request for comment.

Joseph Geevarghese, executive director of Our Revolution – a group that works to elect progressive candidates – said there's a double-standard when progressives win against establishment candidates.

"The establishment expects progressives to fall in line when they prevail at the ballot box, but when progressives win, there are some signs of unity, but the entire establishment doesn't really fall in lockstep behind our candidates," he said. "I think that hurts our ability to do job No. 1, which is to beat the Republicans in November."

Others see the tensions differently.

"When you run a campaign that completely shits on the establishment and then you win that campaign ... ‌then you turn around and say, 'I need this machine in order to win,' it is a little bit disingenuous," Democratic consultant Rodell Mollineau said.

TARGETING DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS 'LIKE ME'

The divisions surfaced ​on Capitol Hill earlier this month when eight moderate Democrats joined Republicans in approving a resolution condemning socialism, drawing criticism from New York democratic socialists Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire ​Valdez, who are poised to win US House seats in November after defeating establishment-backed rivals in their primaries.

"This resolution was aimed squarely at ​democratic socialists like me," Chevalier said in a statement. "We don't need a tent that shrinks from its own history. We need a unified party that takes on corporate power, gets money out of politics and delivers for working people."

In Florida, Democratic Senate nominee Angie Nixon, a democratic socialist, defeated the better-funded retired Lieutenant Colonel Alex ​Vindman by a double-digit margin in August.

Vindman said he would stand beside her "in ​the fight against" Republican Senator Ashley Moody and has donated $825,000 to help Democratic candidates, including $400,000 to the state party to support Nixon and other Florida Democrats.

But it's less clear whether the party is as supportive of Nixon as Vindman has been.

Derrick Scott, chair of Florida's Escambia County Democratic Party, said the party's "vote blue no matter who" message, shorthand for supporting Democratic candidates, appears to come with an exception now that Nixon is the nominee.

"We still have yet to see Nikki Fried, the chair of the Florida Democratic Party, come out and unequivocally and ​full-throatedly support Angie Nixon," he said.

A Democratic Party spokesperson said it's inaccurate to say the party hasn't rallied ‌behind Nixon, noting Fried recently joined Nixon and another statewide candidate for a joint press conference. The spokesperson said the party is working closely with Nixon and is frequently in touch with her team.

Chanae Jackson, the Nixon campaign's former organizing director, said ​voters are frustrated with party leaders who underestimated Nixon and Democratic organizations too often seek Black voter turnout without building durable support for Black-led campaigns.

"They want our labor, but they don't want our leadership," she said. "They want us to work like a ​dog while they take credit for it."

title: Former Texas A&M coach reportedly eyeing a return to Florida State

Before Mike Elko was officially hired as Texas A&M's head coach just weeks before the conclusion of the 2023 regular season, Jimbo Fisher was the king of College Station for nearly six full seasons, leading the Aggies to three consecutive bowl game appearances during his first three seasons; but after finishing 9-1 during the COVID-shortened 2020 season, Fisher's massive extension became a bad omen for the veteran head coach.

According to Yahoo Sports and The Athletic, Florida State coach Mike Norvell's shaky future at the helm could lead to Jimbo Fisher returning as the program's head coach, a job he held for eight seasons after replacing legendary head coach Bobby Bowden, winning the 2013 national title and making the College Football Playoff once.

According to both sources, Fisher "really wants the job," and based on his recent comments about wanting to return to coaching, adjusting his outlook to the current chaotic college football landscape is vital if he has any legitimate shot at returning to the Power Four level.
